Fitting fitness as a sum of per-mutation contributions across all the clones turns the whole plate into data, and the next library becomes a designed set of combinations rather than a fresh random one. The other options each describe a change the method does not make.

what_directed_evolution_requires.question: ProSAR writes each clone's fitness as a sum of per-mutation contributions. Where does that break down?

choices.A: At surface positions, where mutations have no effect at all
choices.B: At active-site residues and at pairs that contact each other
choices.C: Whenever more than two mutations are present in one clone
choices.D: Whenever the mutations are transversions rather than transitions
choices.E: It does not break down, as fitness is additive by definition

what_directed_evolution_requires.explanation: Additivity says a mutation contributes the same amount whatever else is present, which holds well enough for most positions but fails where residues interact: in the active site, and between residues in direct structural contact. That is why the model is a useful approximation to be tested rather than trusted. Surface positions are where additivity works best, and the substitution class and the count of mutations are beside the point.

what_directed_evolution_requires.topic: Reading a contribution out of two measured clones
what_directed_evolution_requires.question: Two esterase clones differ only in that the second also carries M358V, with improvements over wild type of 0.3 and 1.0. What is M358V worth, and why is that notable?

choices.A: 1.3, and it was measured directly in a single mutant clone
choices.B: 0.3, which is the fitness of the clone that lacks it
choices.C: 3.3, the ratio between the two measured improvements
choices.D: 0.7 by subtraction, though that single mutant was never built
choices.E: It cannot be found, as the clones differ at several positions

what_directed_evolution_requires.explanation: Under additivity the two equations differ only in the M358V term, so subtracting gives 1.0 minus 0.3. The point of the method is that this number comes out of clones built for other reasons, and the single mutant was never made. Adding instead of subtracting, taking a ratio of quantities that enter as a sum, or reporting the other clone's fitness all miss that, and the premise states the clones differ only in that mutation.

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.topic: Identifying where a sensor's threshold lives
tuning_a_circuit_threshold.question: In a repressor-promoter sensor, at which step is the ligand concentration that triggers the response actually decided?

choices.A: At the ribosome binding site in front of the reporter gene
choices.B: At the origin of replication setting the plasmid copy number
choices.C: At the promoter's contact with RNA polymerase holoenzyme
choices.D: At the maturation of the fluorescent reporter protein
choices.E: Where the repressor binds the ligand and changes conformation

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.explanation: The concentration at which the circuit flips is decided where the ligand is actually read, which is the repressor's binding site for it. Everything downstream converts that same decision into more or less signal: the ribosome binding site, the copy number and the promoter all scale the output without moving the point at which it appears, and maturation changes when you see the signal rather than at what concentration.

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.topic: Predicting the effect of changing the reporter's RBS
tuning_a_circuit_threshold.question: A TetR-Ptet reporter gets a stronger ribosome binding site. What happens to its dose-response curve?

choices.A: It shifts toward lower inducer concentrations than before
choices.B: It rises at every concentration, turning on at the same one
choices.C: It shifts toward higher inducer concentrations than before
choices.D: It grows steeper without any change in its height
choices.E: It disappears, as the reporter is no longer regulated

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.explanation: A stronger ribosome binding site makes more reporter protein per message, so the whole curve scales up, baseline included, while the concentration at which the repressor lets go is untouched because nothing about ligand binding changed. A horizontal shift in either direction would require changing how the ligand is sensed, a steeper transition is a change in cooperativity, and regulation is unaffected.

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.topic: Separating instrument sensitivity from circuit threshold
tuning_a_circuit_threshold.question: When is it true that a biosensor's detection limit can be improved with a better plate reader?

choices.A: Always, since detection limit is a property of the measurement
choices.B: Never, since instrument sensitivity affects no measurement at all
choices.C: Only for enzymatic reporters, and not for fluorescent ones
choices.D: Only when the reporter sits on a high copy number plasmid
choices.E: When the signal is too faint to read, not when the circuit is silent

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.explanation: Two different limits wear the same name. If the circuit does respond but the output falls below what the instrument can resolve, better optics help; if the repressor does not register the ligand at that concentration there is no signal to amplify and the instrument is irrelevant. The reporter chemistry and the copy number do not decide which of the two limits is binding.

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.question: Two sensor variants turn on at the same ligand concentration, but one reaches a tenfold higher maximum. Which quantity differs?

choices.A: The affinity of the repressor for its ligand
choices.B: The cooperativity of repressor binding at the operator
choices.C: The concentration at which the circuit is detected to respond
choices.D: The dynamic range, which depends on reporter expression
choices.E: Nothing measurable, as the two are equivalent sensors

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.explanation: Identical turn-on points mean the sensing step is the same in both, so the difference lies downstream in how much reporter a derepressed promoter makes. Affinity and threshold are the quantities the question states are unchanged, cooperativity would alter the steepness of the transition rather than its height, and a tenfold difference in maximum is plainly measurable.

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.topic: Reading which feature of a transfer function changed
tuning_a_circuit_threshold.question: A modified sensor goes from barely on to fully on over a narrower range, with the midpoint and maximum unchanged. What was altered?

choices.A: The repressor's ligand affinity, which sets the midpoint
choices.B: The strength of the ribosome binding site on the reporter
choices.C: The maturation rate of the fluorescent reporter protein
choices.D: The copy number of the plasmid carrying the reporter
choices.E: The cooperativity, rather than the threshold or the output level

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.explanation: Three features of a transfer function move independently: where it turns on, how high it goes, and how sharply it makes the transition. Only the third changed here, which is cooperativity, arising from multiple operator sites or from oligomeric repressor binding. Affinity sets the midpoint, which is stated to be unchanged, the ribosome binding site and copy number rescale the height, and maturation affects timing.

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.question: You raise expression of the repressor severalfold and change nothing else. What happens to the dose-response curve?

choices.A: It shifts higher, as more inducer is needed to relieve repression
choices.B: It shifts lower, as more protein is there to bind the ligand
choices.C: Its maximum output rises with no shift along the axis
choices.D: It is unaffected, since the repressor's affinity is unchanged
choices.E: Its baseline rises, because excess repressor becomes leaky

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.explanation: Affinity is unchanged, but there is more repressor to titrate, so a higher inducer concentration is needed before enough of it lets go to turn the promoter on. This is one of the few changes outside the binding site that genuinely moves a threshold, and it is why repressor dosage must be held constant when affinity variants are compared. More repressor tightens rather than loosens the off state.

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.question: Variant one turns on at 1 micromolar and plateaus at 5000 units; variant two turns on at 10 micromolar with the same plateau. Which detects a 2 micromolar sample?

choices.A: Variant two, as a higher threshold gives a cleaner background
choices.B: Either one, since both reach the same maximum signal
choices.C: Neither, as a 5000 unit plateau is too low to read reliably
choices.D: Variant two, as its curve sits where the assay is most accurate
choices.E: Variant one, as 2 micromolar is above its threshold alone

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.explanation: At 2 micromolar variant one is responding and variant two has not begun, so only one of them reports anything at all. The matched plateaus are the distraction here: equal maximum output says nothing about where the response begins. The cleaner-background and accuracy arguments assert benefits not in evidence, and a plateau is not a limitation on reading the signal.

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.topic: Inferring which component changed from a shifted curve
tuning_a_circuit_threshold.question: After a round of mutagenesis on the repressor, a variant's curve shifts to lower ligand with the same maximum. What does that indicate?

choices.A: The repressor now binds its ligand more tightly than before
choices.B: The plasmid is being maintained at a higher copy number
choices.C: The reporter protein folds and matures faster than before
choices.D: The reporter gene is being translated more efficiently now
choices.E: The promoter has lost one of its operator sites entirely

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.explanation: A horizontal shift with the height unchanged points at the sensing step, and since the mutagenesis was aimed at the repressor the straightforward reading is tighter ligand binding, so less ligand is needed to derepress. Translation, copy number and maturation would all change the height or the timing instead, and losing an operator would raise the baseline toward constitutive expression.

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.topic: Designing a campaign to retune a sensor
tuning_a_circuit_threshold.question: You want a repressor that responds to a new small molecule and not to the original one. Which design fits?

choices.A: One round of mutagenesis, picking the brightest colony on the new ligand
choices.B: A library of reporter ribosome binding sites read with the new ligand
choices.C: Raising the copy number of the sensor plasmid and remeasuring
choices.D: Replacing the reporter with a marker and plating on the old ligand
choices.E: Mutagenize the binding domain, positive on new, negative on old, iterate

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.explanation: Two things are asked for at once, gaining a response to the new ligand and losing the response to the old, and that pair of requirements is what a dual selection is for; iteration is needed because a specificity shift is usually built from several mutations. Testing only the gain in one round leaves wild type in the pool, the ribosome binding site and copy number change output rather than specificity, and plating on the old ligand selects against what you want to keep.

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.topic: Recognizing which changes cannot move a threshold
tuning_a_circuit_threshold.question: Several groups report sensors with shifted thresholds. Which reported change could not, on its own, have moved one?

choices.A: A brighter reporter protein in place of the original one
choices.B: A repressor variant with altered ligand dissociation kinetics
choices.C: A severalfold change in how much repressor is expressed
choices.D: Substitutions in the ligand-binding pocket of the repressor
choices.E: A chimeric repressor with a binding domain from a homolog

tuning_a_circuit_threshold.explanation: Swapping in a brighter reporter multiplies the output of a decision already made, so the curve rises without moving along the concentration axis. The other four all act on how the ligand is read or how much repressor must be titrated: pocket substitutions, altered binding kinetics, a swapped binding domain, and repressor dosage can each change the concentration at which the circuit responds.

reporters_and_normalization.question: What does a flow cytometer report for each cell that passes the laser?

choices.A: Forward scatter, side scatter and one or more fluorescence signals
choices.B: The total fluorescence of the culture divided by its optical density
choices.C: A timelapse of that cell's fluorescence over several generations
choices.D: The subcellular location of the fluorescent protein in that cell
choices.E: The absorbance of the cell at six hundred nanometers

reporters_and_normalization.explanation: Cells pass the beam one at a time, so each one gives scatter in the forward and side directions plus whatever fluorescence channels the instrument carries. A culture-level ratio is what a fluorimeter and an OD reading give, a timelapse and subcellular detail require microscopy, and absorbance at six hundred nanometers is a bulk density measurement rather than anything recorded per cell.

reporters_and_normalization.question: How does FACS differ from ordinary analytical flow cytometry?

choices.A: FACS measures scatter while cytometry measures only fluorescence
choices.B: FACS works on bacteria while cytometry works only on mammalian cells
choices.C: FACS requires a fluorogenic substrate rather than a fluorescent protein
choices.D: FACS reports a population average instead of single-cell values
choices.E: FACS recovers the cell population you want, rather than just reading it

reporters_and_normalization.explanation: Both instruments read the same per-cell signals; the difference is that sorting physically diverts the cells you selected into a tube so you can grow them, which is what makes it an enrichment step rather than a measurement. Both are used mainly on mammalian cells and both work on bacteria and yeast with care, and neither is restricted to a particular kind of reporter.

reporters_and_normalization.question: You need to follow fluorescence in the same cells over several divisions. Which instrument does that, and why?

choices.A: Cytometry, since it gives precise per-cell values quickly
choices.B: A fluorimeter, since it follows a culture continuously over time
choices.C: A plate reader, since it can read the same well repeatedly
choices.D: Microscopy, since cytometry gives one timepoint per cell only
choices.E: Either instrument, since both track individual cells over time

reporters_and_normalization.explanation: A cytometer destroys the arrangement it measures: a cell passes the laser once and is gone, so you get a single timepoint per cell. Cells immobilized on an agar pad can be imaged repeatedly, which is what allows timelapse, lineage tracking and correlation of morphology with signal, at the cost of throughput and precision. Culture-level instruments cannot resolve individual cells at all.

reporters_and_normalization.question: Two cultures of the same strain are read on a fluorimeter, one twice as concentrated as the other. Why must the signal be divided by OD?

choices.A: Because autofluorescence from tryptophan scales with the signal
choices.B: Because fluorescence scales with concentration, not brightness per cell
choices.C: Because the excitation and emission wavelengths differ in the two samples
choices.D: Because optical density is measured at a longer wavelength than emission
choices.E: Because the fluorimeter cannot read absorbance and fluorescence together

reporters_and_normalization.explanation: Fluorescence from a bulk sample is linear in how many cells are in the beam, so the denser culture gives roughly twice the signal from cells that are no brighter at all. Dividing by optical density converts the reading into a per-cell quantity, which is the comparison you meant to make. Autofluorescence is a separate background problem, and a fluorimeter does read absorbance as well.

reporters_and_normalization.question: Sample one reads 0.86 fluorescence at OD 0.44 and sample two reads 0.42 at OD 0.22. What do you conclude?

choices.A: Sample one is about twice as bright per cell as sample two
choices.B: The two express the reporter at about the same level per cell
choices.C: Sample two expresses the reporter about twice as strongly per cell
choices.D: Nothing, since the two optical densities are not identical
choices.E: Sample one has about twice the plasmid copy number of sample two

reporters_and_normalization.explanation: The ratios are 0.86 over 0.44 and 0.42 over 0.22, which come to about 2.0 and 1.9, so the cells are equally bright and the only difference is that one culture is twice as dense. Reading the raw fluorescence instead is exactly the error normalization prevents. Differing optical densities are not an obstacle, since dividing by them is the point, and nothing here speaks to copy number.

reporters_and_normalization.topic: Knowing which readouts require OD normalization
reporters_and_normalization.question: Which readout requires normalization for optical density, and which does not?

choices.A: Both fluorimetry and microscopy require optical density normalization
choices.B: Neither requires it, provided the signal itself is normalized
choices.C: Microscopy requires it; fluorimetry reports per-cell values already
choices.D: Fluorimetry requires it; microscopy already resolves single cells
choices.E: Only enzymatic reporter assays require it, not fluorescent ones

reporters_and_normalization.explanation: Ensemble measurements sum over however many cells are present, so a fluorimeter reading has to be divided by density to become a per-cell number. Microscopy and cytometry already resolve individual cells, so there is nothing to divide out, although both still need the signal itself normalized against a standard so that readings taken on different days can be compared.

reporters_and_normalization.topic: Matching enzymatic reporters to their substrates
reporters_and_normalization.question: Which pairing of reporter gene and readout is correct?

choices.A: lacZ with nitrocefin, which turns yellow upon hydrolysis
choices.B: bla with Xgal, which turns blue when the lactam is opened
choices.C: phoA with oNPG, since phosphatases cleave galactosides
choices.D: lacZ with Xgal, oNPG or Sgal, giving blue, yellow or black
choices.E: bla with Sgal, which turns black when galactose is released

reporters_and_normalization.explanation: Beta-galactosidase hydrolyzes galactose from its substrate, and the same chemistry is available in several colors: Xgal gives blue, oNPG yellow and Sgal black, with fluorogenic versions for cytometry and microscopy. Replacing the galactose with phosphate gives the corresponding alkaline phosphatase substrates, while beta-lactamase is read with lactam substrates such as nitrocefin and has a narrower set.

reporters_and_normalization.topic: Explaining the sensitivity of enzymatic reporters
reporters_and_normalization.question: Why is an enzymatic reporter often more sensitive than a fluorescent protein?

choices.A: Because the enzyme is expressed from a stronger promoter
choices.B: Because one enzyme converts many substrate molecules over time
choices.C: Because enzymes fold faster than fluorescent proteins do
choices.D: Because the substrate is consumed stoichiometrically with enzyme
choices.E: Because enzymatic readouts need no normalization of signal

reporters_and_normalization.explanation: A fluorescent protein gives one unit of signal per molecule, while an enzyme keeps turning over substrate for as long as the assay runs, so a small amount of protein builds a large amount of product. That amplification is why these assays are often more precise and sensitive. Stoichiometric consumption would remove the amplification, and the promoter and folding are not what distinguishes the two.

reporters_and_normalization.topic: Reasoning about a two-stain viability assay
reporters_and_normalization.question: A viability kit pairs propidium iodide with SYTO 9. How does the pair report the dead fraction?

choices.A: Propidium iodide enters all cells; SYTO 9 enters only dead ones
choices.B: Both stains enter all cells, and the dead ones bind more of each
choices.C: SYTO 9 stains the medium, so dead cells appear as dark gaps
choices.D: Propidium iodide enters only cells whose membrane has failed
choices.E: Propidium iodide is enzymatically activated inside living cells

reporters_and_normalization.explanation: The logic rests on permeability: SYTO 9 crosses intact membranes and so labels the whole population, while propidium iodide is excluded from live cells and enters only those whose membrane has been compromised. Cells carrying both signals are the dead fraction, read per cell by cytometry or microscopy. Reversing the two permeabilities inverts the assay, and no enzymatic activation is involved.

reporters_and_normalization.topic: Recognizing growth-phase artifacts in a normalized assay
reporters_and_normalization.question: Your normalized reporter signal differs between two strains, and one grows more slowly. Why is that comparison treacherous?

choices.A: Because slower growth lowers the optical density below readable range
choices.B: Because normalization is invalid whenever growth rates differ at all
choices.C: Because slower cultures autofluoresce more strongly than faster ones
choices.D: Because cell size and expression rates both shift with growth phase
choices.E: Because fluorescence is not linear in concentration during lag phase

reporters_and_normalization.explanation: Bacteria are different sizes at different points in growth, and replication, transcription and translation all run at different rates, so two strains sampled at the same optical density may not be in comparable physiological states. The honest fix is to sample at matched growth stages and interpret with care rather than to elaborate the arithmetic. Normalization is still worth doing, and the remaining claims are invented.

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.topic: Telling the three experiment shapes apart
differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.question: A device is assayed in rich medium and in phosphate buffer, with nothing else varied. Which shape of experiment is that?

choices.A: A transfer function, since two input levels are compared
choices.B: A dynamics experiment, since medium changes over the growth
choices.C: A differential expression experiment, comparing two conditions
choices.D: A heterogeneity experiment, since cells differ between media
choices.E: A dose-response, since buffer is a diluted form of the medium

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.explanation: Differential expression means two or more discrete conditions compared against each other to ask whether the device behaves differently in them. A transfer function needs a graded series of one input rather than two separate media, a dynamics experiment follows one condition over time, and heterogeneity is about variation between cells within a single sample.

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.question: What distinguishes a transfer function experiment from a differential expression experiment?

choices.A: The stimulus is graded, giving a function relating input to output
choices.B: The readout is fluorescence rather than an enzymatic product
choices.C: The measurement is made on single cells rather than on a culture
choices.D: The experiment runs over time rather than at one timepoint
choices.E: The device is compared against a constitutive reference strain

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.explanation: Both relate an input to a measured response; the difference is that a transfer function varies the input across a graded series, usually a dilution series of an inducer, so what comes out is a curve rather than a comparison of two points. The readout, the instrument and the presence of a reference strain can be the same in either shape of experiment.

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.topic: Designing the input series for a transfer function
differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.question: You are measuring the response of an arabinose promoter across concentrations. How should the series be spaced?

choices.A: Evenly in concentration, so the steps are equal in size
choices.B: In a fourfold dilution series, spanning several decades
choices.C: At two concentrations, the highest and the lowest usable
choices.D: Randomly, so that no concentration biases the fitted curve
choices.E: Clustered at the top, where the output is largest and clearest

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.explanation: A transfer function is read on a logarithmic concentration axis because the response spans orders of magnitude, so a constant-fold dilution series puts the points at even spacing along the axis that matters and captures both the baseline and the plateau. Even spacing in concentration crowds nearly every point into the top decade, and two points cannot define a curve at all.

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.topic: Knowing which control a differential experiment needs
differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.question: Why does a strain carrying a candidate inducible promoter have to be assayed alongside a constitutive one in the same conditions?

choices.A: To establish the maximum output the host can sustain
choices.B: To normalize for optical density across the two conditions
choices.C: To confirm the inducible promoter's sequence is correct
choices.D: To check the reporter folds correctly in both media
choices.E: To separate a real response from an effect of the condition itself

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.explanation: A condition can change the reading for reasons that have nothing to do with the promoter under test, by altering growth, expression capacity, or the fluorescence of the medium. A constitutive reporter run in the same conditions shows what the condition does to a promoter that cannot respond, so a change seen only in the inducible strain is attributable to induction. Density normalization is a separate step applied to both strains.

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.topic: Interpreting a differential experiment with its control
differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.question: Adding salt raises the inducible strain's signal and leaves the constitutive strain's unchanged, with density held constant. What does that show?

choices.A: Salt quenches the fluorescence of the reporter protein
choices.B: Salt slows growth, which concentrates the reporter in the cells
choices.C: The result is inconclusive without following it over time
choices.D: The inducible promoter responds to salt, as intended
choices.E: Salt raises fluorescence generally, in both of the strains

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.explanation: The control strain is the test of whether the condition itself moved the reading, and it did not, so the rise in the inducible strain is a response of that promoter. Quenching would lower rather than raise the signal, growth effects are excluded because the densities are matched, and a general effect of salt would have shown up in the control. A time course would add information without being needed for this conclusion.

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.topic: Choosing an instrument for single-cell dynamics
differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.question: An oscillating circuit must be followed in single cells over time. Why is microscopy the only practical readout?

choices.A: Because oscillations are too fast for a cytometer to sample
choices.B: Because oscillations only appear in cells immobilized on agar
choices.C: Because oscillating circuits use reporters a cytometer cannot see
choices.D: Because a plate reader averages away the oscillation entirely
choices.E: Because a cytometer reads each cell once and cannot revisit it

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.explanation: Following a trajectory means measuring the same cell repeatedly, and a cytometer sees each cell exactly once as it passes the beam. Immobilized cells can be imaged over and over, which is what makes the time axis available. A plate reader does average over the population, which is a real limitation, but it is not the reason microscopy rather than cytometry is required.

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.topic: Recognizing the limits of a bulk measurement
differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.question: A pathway is expressed in only about a tenth of the cells. What does a plate reader measurement of the culture show?

choices.A: A bimodal signal revealing the two subpopulations present
choices.B: A signal about a tenth of the fully induced level, with no hint why
choices.C: No signal at all, since the majority of cells are silent
choices.D: The same signal as a uniformly expressing culture of equal mean
choices.E: A signal that fluctuates as the subpopulations interconvert

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.explanation: A bulk instrument returns one number for the whole sample, so a tenth of the cells expressing strongly reads the same as every cell expressing weakly. The reduced signal is visible but its cause is not, which is precisely why heterogeneity has to be chased with a single-cell method. A bulk reading cannot be bimodal, and a culture with the same mean is exactly what it cannot be told apart from.

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.topic: Recognizing which properties can be followed over time
differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.question: Why is it impractical to follow single-cell dynamics of a cell making a biofuel?

choices.A: Because biofuel production is too slow to resolve in a timelapse
choices.B: Because the product leaves the cell and so cannot be imaged in it
choices.C: Because timelapse readouts are restricted to fluorescence signals
choices.D: Because microscopy cannot be done on cells producing solvents
choices.E: Because the biofuel quenches any fluorescent reporter present

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.explanation: A timelapse needs a signal that can be read optically from the same cell again and again without destroying it, and in practice that means fluorescence. A metabolite has to be extracted and run on an instrument, which consumes the sample and ends the trajectory. The product diffusing out is a real complication for a different reason, and the remaining claims are invented.

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.question: Four strains are grown with and without arabinose, and for one of them induction drops the growth rate about fourfold. What does that show?

choices.A: That the induced component is toxic to the cell when expressed
choices.B: That arabinose itself is toxic to that particular strain
choices.C: That the promoter in that strain is leakier than in the others
choices.D: That the reporter signal in that strain will be artifactually high
choices.E: That the strain has lost its plasmid during the induction

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.explanation: Following optical density over time gives a growth rate, and comparing induced against uninduced for the same strain isolates the effect of expressing the component. The other three strains carry the same sugar and the same promoter and are unaffected, which rules out the sugar and points at the component itself. Toxicity in fact tends to distort normalized activity rather than simply raise it.

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.topic: Matching the experiment shape to the question asked
differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.question: You want to know the inducer concentration at which a sensor reaches half its maximum output. Which experiment answers that?

choices.A: Two conditions, with and without the inducer present
choices.B: A timelapse of single cells carrying the sensor construct
choices.C: A cytometry histogram of the fully induced population
choices.D: A graded inducer series read as a transfer function
choices.E: A growth curve with and without the inducer added

differential_expression_and_transfer_fun.explanation: A half-maximal point is a feature of a curve, so you need the curve: a graded series of inducer concentrations with the output measured at each one. Two conditions give you only the endpoints and cannot locate the midpoint between them, a histogram describes the spread at one concentration, and a timelapse and a growth curve answer questions about time and fitness rather than about dose.

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.topic: Understanding why retention is scored without selection
population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.question: To score what fraction of a culture still carries a plasmid, you plate on agar without antibiotic. Why leave the drug out?

choices.A: Because the antibiotic would interfere with the reporter signal
choices.B: Because plasmid-free cells must be able to form colonies too
choices.C: Because the drug degrades during the incubation anyway
choices.D: Because antibiotic plates give smaller and harder colonies
choices.E: Because the plasmid is lost faster in the presence of the drug

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.explanation: The quantity you want is the proportion of the population that has lost the plasmid, so those cells have to survive long enough to be counted. On a selective plate they never form colonies, and every colony you count carries the plasmid by construction, which makes the measured retention one hundred percent whatever the truth is. The drug does not degrade or alter the reporter on this timescale.

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.topic: Recognizing a measurement that destroys its own population
population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.question: A proposal grows the culture in antibiotic throughout and counts fluorescent colonies on selective plates at each timepoint. What is wrong?

choices.A: Nothing, provided enough timepoints are taken across the growth
choices.B: Fluorescence cannot be scored on plates containing antibiotic
choices.C: The plasmid-free cells are killed before they can be counted
choices.D: Colony counts are too imprecise to estimate a rate of loss
choices.E: The antibiotic selects for plasmids with higher copy number

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.explanation: Selection removes the very subpopulation whose appearance you are trying to time, so the surviving population is plasmid-bearing by definition and no rate can be inferred from it. This is the same survivor-bias logic as recovering a library of toxic variants after an overnight outgrowth: the population you measure is the one that survived the measurement.

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.topic: Understanding the reference in a digital droplet measurement
population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.question: Digital droplet PCR quantifies a plasmid-borne gene against a chromosomal locus. What does the chromosomal target provide?

choices.A: A positive control showing the PCR reaction worked at all
choices.B: A measure of how much DNA was lost during the extraction
choices.C: A sequence against which the plasmid primers are designed
choices.D: A per-genome denominator, so the result is copies per cell
choices.E: A check that the plasmid has not recombined into the genome

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.explanation: Counting plasmid molecules alone tells you how much plasmid was in the tube, which depends on how many cells you extracted and how well the extraction worked. Dividing by a single-copy chromosomal locus converts the count into plasmid copies per genome, which is the quantity that can be compared between timepoints. Extraction losses affect both targets and so divide out, which is part of why the ratio works.

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.topic: Using single-cell distributions to see a subpopulation
population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.question: Why does flow cytometry detect a growing plasmid-free fraction that a plate reader misses?

choices.A: Because it resolves the population into two distinct peaks
choices.B: Because cytometry does not require normalization for density
choices.C: Because cytometry is more sensitive to dim fluorescence signals
choices.D: Because it counts colonies rather than averaging over a culture
choices.E: Because plate readers cannot read green fluorescent protein

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.explanation: A culture containing bright and dark cells reads on a plate reader as one intermediate number, indistinguishable from every cell being moderately bright. Cytometry reports a value per cell, so the two groups appear as separate peaks whose relative areas give the fraction directly. Sensitivity is not the issue, and cytometry counts cells rather than colonies.

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.topic: Recognizing valid approaches to measuring retention
population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.question: Which combination of methods can each, on its own, give a plasmid-loss rate over time?

choices.A: Selective plating, bulk fluorescence, and growth rate measurement
choices.B: Non-selective plating, single-cell cytometry, and droplet PCR
choices.C: Cycle sequencing, colony PCR, and restriction digest of isolates
choices.D: Microscopy of a single timepoint, plus a final endpoint plate count
choices.E: Optical density over time, plus the doubling time of the host

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.explanation: Each of the three counts the plasmid-bearing share of the population in a different currency: colonies scored for fluorescence on a plate where both kinds can grow, cells scored individually by their fluorescence, and plasmid molecules scored against a chromosomal reference. Selective plating removes the subpopulation of interest, and growth or density measurements describe the culture without resolving who carries what.

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.topic: Distinguishing heterogeneity from a shifted mean
population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.question: Two cultures give the same mean reporter signal, but one is uniform and the other is a mix of bright and dark cells. Which measurement tells them apart?

choices.A: A fluorimeter reading normalized for optical density
choices.B: A growth curve followed through to stationary phase
choices.C: An enzymatic reporter assay read on a plate reader
choices.D: A single-cell readout such as cytometry or microscopy
choices.E: Digital droplet PCR against a chromosomal reference

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.explanation: Any instrument that sums over the sample returns the mean and nothing else, so two populations with the same mean are identical to it by construction. Only a readout that reports per cell can show that one distribution is narrow and the other has two modes. Droplet PCR counts molecules rather than describing how expression is distributed among cells.

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.topic: Designing a time course for plasmid loss
population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.question: How should a culture be handled across a retention time course?

choices.A: Grown without selection and sampled repeatedly as it passages
choices.B: Grown with selection and sampled only at the final timepoint
choices.C: Grown without selection but sampled once, at stationary phase
choices.D: Grown with selection, diluting into fresh drug at each sampling
choices.E: Grown without selection and plated only on selective agar

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.explanation: Loss accumulates over generations, so the culture has to be passaged without selection and sampled along the way, which gives the fraction as a function of how many doublings have elapsed. Selection at any stage removes the cells you are counting, a single endpoint gives one fraction and so no rate, and plating on selective agar discards the plasmid-free colonies at the final step.

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.topic: Interpreting fluorescent and non-fluorescent colony counts
population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.question: After twenty generations without selection, a non-selective plate shows 180 fluorescent and 20 non-fluorescent colonies. What is the plasmid-free fraction?

choices.A: 20 / 180, the non-fluorescent against the fluorescent count
choices.B: 20 / 20, since only the non-fluorescent colonies are counted
choices.C: 180 / 200, the fluorescent share of all the colonies counted
choices.D: 20 / 200, the non-fluorescent share of all colonies counted
choices.E: 20 / 20 x 180, the counts combined across both classes

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.explanation: A fraction of the population is the count of interest over the total counted, so the plasmid-free share is twenty out of the two hundred colonies on the plate. Dividing by the fluorescent count alone gives an odds ratio rather than a fraction, and the fluorescent share answers the complementary question of how many still carry the plasmid.

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.question: A subpopulation has stopped expressing a pathway. How would you tell a mutation from a regulatory switch?

choices.A: Repeat the cytometry with a brighter fluorescent reporter
choices.B: Sort the dark cells, regrow them, and see whether they stay dark
choices.C: Compare the bulk signal against an uninduced control culture
choices.D: Follow the optical density of the culture over several passages
choices.E: Measure the plasmid copy number by droplet PCR on the culture

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.explanation: A mutation is heritable and a regulatory state usually is not, so isolating the dark cells and letting them grow up distinguishes the two: a population that stays dark has changed its sequence, while one that recovers a mixture was switching. Sequencing the sorted cells settles it outright. Brighter reporters, bulk comparisons and density measurements cannot address heredity at all.

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.topic: Reasoning about the consequence of a silent subpopulation
population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.question: A tenth of the cells carry out a biosynthesis and the rest do not. Why does that matter beyond the lower titer?

choices.A: Because the non-producers will outgrow the producers over time
choices.B: Because the pathway genes will be lost from the population entirely
choices.C: Because the producing cells must be sorted before every assay
choices.D: Because bulk assays report the shortfall without revealing its cause
choices.E: Because titer cannot be measured at all in a mixed population

population_measurements_and_plasmid_rete.explanation: The diagnosis is what is at stake. A bulk measurement shows output below expectation, which looks the same as every cell working badly, and those two situations call for opposite fixes: one is a problem of expression in a subpopulation and the other of pathway flux. Non-producers often do grow faster, since they carry less burden, but that is a separate consequence rather than the measurement problem.

extraction_and_purification.topic: Recognizing the shape of an in vitro assay
extraction_and_purification.question: Every in vitro assay in this course has the same two steps. What are they?

choices.A: Grow the culture to saturation, then read the optical density
choices.B: Purify the component of interest, then observe what you purified
choices.C: Lyse the cells, then transform the lysate into a fresh host
choices.D: Label the component, then follow it inside the living cell
choices.E: Sequence the construct, then confirm it matches the design

extraction_and_purification.explanation: First you separate the thing you care about from everything else, which destroys the cells and is why these are called in vitro assays, and then you look at its activity, its structure, or simply how much of it there is. The first half of the problem is the purifying and the second half is the looking, and nearly every method in the lecture is one or the other.

extraction_and_purification.topic: Knowing what a methanol extraction recovers
extraction_and_purification.question: You add methanol to a cell pellet to recover a small-molecule product. What does the methanol do to the rest of the cell?

choices.A: It denatures the membranes while keeping proteins soluble
choices.B: It solubilizes nucleic acids and leaves the proteins intact
choices.C: It precipitates protein and nucleic acid, which stay behind
choices.D: It digests the cell wall so the contents can be decanted
choices.E: It converts the product to a more volatile derivative

extraction_and_purification.explanation: An organic solvent that dissolves small molecules will not keep large charged polymers in solution, so protein and nucleic acid crash out and the metabolites come away in the supernatant. That is what makes it a selective first step rather than a general lysis. Acetone, chloroform-methanol and the Bligh-Dyer method work on the same principle for different classes of compound.

extraction_and_purification.topic: Choosing a lysis method for the component wanted
extraction_and_purification.question: You need active enzyme from a cell pellet. Why is sonication appropriate and alkaline lysis not?

choices.A: Alkaline lysis denatures protein, while sonication breaks cells open
choices.B: Alkaline lysis cannot break the cell wall of E. coli at all
choices.C: Sonication is gentler on small molecules than alkali is
choices.D: Alkaline lysis requires a French press to complete the lysis
choices.E: Sonication selectively releases cytoplasmic over periplasmic protein

extraction_and_purification.explanation: Alkaline lysis is a denaturing method, which is exactly what you want when the thing you are recovering is plasmid DNA and the protein is in the way, and exactly what you must avoid when the protein is the product. Sonication, osmotic shock, freeze-thaw, lysozyme, detergent, bead milling and the French press all break cells without destroying what is inside.

extraction_and_purification.topic: Knowing what an ion exchange column separates on
extraction_and_purification.question: A column is packed with beads carrying amino groups. Which species are retained longest?

choices.A: The largest species, since they cannot enter the bead pores
choices.B: The most hydrophobic species, which partition into the resin
choices.C: The smallest species, which penetrate furthest into the beads
choices.D: Whichever species carries an affinity tag for those groups
choices.E: The negatively charged species, attracted to the positive support

extraction_and_purification.explanation: Amino groups make the support positively charged, so negatively charged molecules are impeded and elute later, which is anion exchange; putting carboxylates on the beads gives the cation exchange counterpart. If retention is strong enough the separation becomes effectively all-or-nothing, so the column can be washed extensively and the product comes off very clean. Size and hydrophobicity are what other column chemistries exploit.

extraction_and_purification.topic: Reasoning about size exclusion elution order
extraction_and_purification.question: In size exclusion chromatography, why do larger molecules come off the column earlier?

choices.A: Because larger molecules diffuse faster through the mobile phase
choices.B: Because the beads bind small molecules through weak interactions
choices.C: Because larger molecules carry more charge and are repelled
choices.D: Because larger molecules reach less of the porous bead interior
choices.E: Because smaller molecules are retained by the frit at the outlet

extraction_and_purification.explanation: The stationary phase is a bead riddled with pores, and the smaller a molecule is the more of that interior volume it can wander into, so it takes a longer path and elutes later. Large molecules are excluded from the pores and travel more or less straight through. Nothing is binding anything here, which is what makes the method so gentle and why the elution order maps onto size.

extraction_and_purification.topic: Matching an affinity ligand to its binding partner
extraction_and_purification.question: Which pairing of immobilized ligand and captured partner is used in affinity chromatography?

choices.A: Glutathione on the resin, capturing glutathione S-transferase fusions
choices.B: Streptavidin on the resin, capturing histidine-tagged proteins
choices.C: Nickel on the resin, capturing chitin binding domain fusions
choices.D: Lectin on the resin, capturing single-stranded nucleic acids
choices.E: Cellulose on the resin, capturing glutathione S-transferase fusions

extraction_and_purification.explanation: Each affinity system pairs a ligand with the domain that binds it: glutathione with GST, chitin with the chitin binding domain, cellulose with the cellulose binding domain, lectins with carbohydrates, and antibodies with their epitopes. The remaining options cross those pairs, matching a resin with a tag that does not bind it, which would wash the target straight through.

extraction_and_purification.topic: Understanding how a bound target is released
extraction_and_purification.question: Your tagged protein is bound to an affinity resin and the contaminants are washed away. How is it released?

choices.A: By raising the ionic strength until the protein precipitates
choices.B: By digesting the resin with a protease specific to the support
choices.C: By running the column backward to reverse the flow direction
choices.D: By adding free ligand to compete it off, or by shifting the pH
choices.E: By heating the column until the interaction becomes unstable

extraction_and_purification.explanation: The target is held by a specific interaction, so the way to let go of it is to compete for the same interaction, usually by flooding the column with the soluble ligand, or to weaken it with a change in pH. That is also why the method cleans so well: everything that was not bound has already been washed through, and the elution is specific to the thing that was.

extraction_and_purification.topic: Inferring oligomeric state from an elution volume
extraction_and_purification.question: A purified 30 kDa protein elutes from a sizing column where a 90 kDa standard elutes. What does that suggest?

choices.A: The protein is a trimer in solution under these conditions
choices.B: The protein has been proteolyzed into smaller fragments
choices.C: The column was overloaded, shifting the elution earlier
choices.D: The protein carries a charge that excludes it from the beads
choices.E: The protein is a monomer that is unusually tightly folded

extraction_and_purification.explanation: A sizing column separates on hydrodynamic size, so a protein running at three times its subunit mass is behaving as a particle three times that size, which for a 30 kDa subunit means three copies traveling together. Proteolysis would move it later rather than earlier, a tightly folded monomer runs at or below its mass, and charge is not what this chemistry responds to.

extraction_and_purification.topic: Choosing a purification from the property exploited
extraction_and_purification.question: You must separate your untagged protein from a contaminant of identical mass but opposite net charge. Which method works?

choices.A: Ion exchange, which retains them differently by their charge
choices.B: Size exclusion, which resolves them by hydrodynamic radius
choices.C: Methanol extraction, which precipitates one but not the other
choices.D: Affinity chromatography on a nickel-charged resin column
choices.E: Solid-phase extraction, which separates them by volatility

extraction_and_purification.explanation: Every purification exploits some property in which the target and the contaminant differ, so the method follows from where the difference lies. Identical mass makes a sizing column useless, and with no tag there is nothing for an affinity resin to grip, while opposite net charge is precisely what an exchange column reads. Methanol would precipitate both proteins together.

extraction_and_purification.topic: Reasoning about the order of purification steps
extraction_and_purification.question: Why is an affinity capture usually run before a sizing column rather than after it?

choices.A: Because sizing columns cannot be loaded with crude cell lysate
choices.B: Because affinity resins are destroyed by concentrated samples
choices.C: Because capture from lysate removes most contaminants in one step
choices.D: Because sizing columns separate better at higher ionic strength
choices.E: Because the affinity tag must be removed before sizing is possible

extraction_and_purification.explanation: An affinity step takes a complex lysate down to nearly pure target in a single pass, which is an enormous reduction in complexity for very little work, so it belongs first. A sizing column is low in capacity and resolves only by size, which makes it a good polishing step on an already simple sample and a poor way to attack a lysate. The tag need not be removed for either step.

detection_and_structure_determination.question: An HPLC with a UV detector gives three peaks. What is plotted, and what identifies a compound?

choices.A: Absorbance against retention time, with retention identifying it
choices.B: Mass against charge, with the ratio identifying the compound
choices.C: Absorbance against wavelength, with the maximum identifying it
choices.D: Concentration against time, with the slope identifying it
choices.E: Retention time against pressure, with the ratio identifying it

detection_and_structure_determination.explanation: The detector watches the eluate as it comes off the column, so the trace is absorbance against the time since injection, and each species appears as a peak at a retention time characteristic of its size, polarity and interaction with the stationary phase. That retention time is reproducible between runs, which is what allows a peak to be assigned by comparison with a standard.

detection_and_structure_determination.topic: Choosing between gas and liquid chromatography
detection_and_structure_determination.question: What distinguishes a GCMS from an LCMS, and what does that imply about the sample?

choices.A: The gas instrument has higher mass resolution than the liquid one
choices.B: The mobile phase is water, so the analyte must be water soluble
choices.C: The gas instrument ionizes the sample and the liquid one does not
choices.D: The gas instrument measures mass and the liquid one measures charge
choices.E: The mobile phase is an inert gas, so the analyte must be volatile

detection_and_structure_determination.explanation: The two setups are very similar apart from what carries the sample through the column: a GCMS uses an inert gas such as helium, which means the analyte has to survive being vaporized, while an LCMS uses a liquid mobile phase and so handles involatile and thermally fragile compounds. Both ionize the eluate and both report mass over charge.

detection_and_structure_determination.topic: Relating mass resolution to the instrument
detection_and_structure_determination.question: A metabolite must be distinguished from a contaminant differing by 0.01 Da. Which instrument can do that?

choices.A: A quadrupole instrument, resolving to about 1 Da
choices.B: A gas chromatograph with a flame ionization detector
choices.C: A triple quadrupole operated in scanning mode
choices.D: An HPLC with ultraviolet absorbance detection
choices.E: An Orbitrap, resolving to about 0.001 Da

detection_and_structure_determination.explanation: Resolution is what decides this, and the instruments differ by three orders of magnitude in it: an Orbitrap resolves to about a thousandth of a dalton, roughly a thousandth of a proton mass, while a quadrupole resolves to about a dalton and would see the two species as one peak. That resolution is also why Orbitraps cost around five times what a quadrupole instrument does.

detection_and_structure_determination.topic: Understanding why quantitation needs an internal standard
detection_and_structure_determination.question: Why does quantitative mass spectrometry require an internal standard rather than a peak area alone?

choices.A: Because the detector saturates at high analyte concentrations
choices.B: Because retention times drift between successive injections
choices.C: Because peak area is proportional to mass rather than to moles
choices.D: Because ionization efficiency varies with sample and run
choices.E: Because the instrument cannot measure absolute mass accurately

detection_and_structure_determination.explanation: How readily a molecule ionizes depends on what else is in the sample and on the state of the source, so the same amount of compound can give different signal from run to run. A standard added in a known amount and carried through the same sample experiences the same conditions, so the ratio of analyte to standard is stable even when the absolute signal is not.

detection_and_structure_determination.question: You have a few milligrams of a purified product at high purity. What does proton NMR tell you?

choices.A: The absolute stereochemistry of every chiral center present
choices.B: The exact mass of the compound to within a millidalton
choices.C: The three-dimensional conformation the molecule adopts in a crystal
choices.D: The concentration of the compound in the original culture
choices.E: The connectivity and the number of hydrogens in each environment

detection_and_structure_determination.explanation: Proton NMR reports on hydrogens in distinct chemical environments, and because the area under a peak is proportional to how many hydrogens give rise to it, you can count them and piece the structure together. That is usually enough to determine a structure, with the standing exceptions of absolute stereochemistry and sometimes isomers. Mass is read on a spectrometer and crystal conformation by diffraction.

detection_and_structure_determination.topic: Knowing the requirement for a diffraction experiment
detection_and_structure_determination.question: What does X-ray crystallography require of the sample that NMR does not?

choices.A: Isotopic labeling of the carbon atoms in the molecule
choices.B: That the compound crystallize, which not everything will do
choices.C: That the compound be volatile enough to enter the gas phase
choices.D: That the compound carry a chromophore absorbing ultraviolet light
choices.E: That the compound be present at micromolar concentration only

detection_and_structure_determination.explanation: Both methods need a clean sample, but diffraction needs that sample arranged in a periodic lattice, and whether a given compound will grow a usable crystal is not something you can count on. When it does, the diffraction pattern yields an electron density map that shows where the atoms sit, which settles absolute stereochemistry and resolves isomer questions that NMR leaves open.

detection_and_structure_determination.topic: Choosing a readout when the reaction is invisible
detection_and_structure_determination.question: A methylation reaction leaves substrate and product absorbing at the same wavelength. Why does that rule out a photometer?

choices.A: Because methyl groups do not absorb ultraviolet light at all
choices.B: Because the reaction runs too slowly to follow in a cuvette
choices.C: Because the product is unstable and decays during the reading
choices.D: Because nothing about the tube changes as the reaction proceeds
choices.E: Because the enzyme itself absorbs more strongly than either

detection_and_structure_determination.explanation: A photometric assay works only when the conversion changes what the sample absorbs. If substrate and product have the same absorbance, the reading is identical before and after and the instrument reports nothing, however well the reaction ran. The way forward is to separate them first, which is what running the mixture on an HPLC and quantifying the product peak accomplishes.

detection_and_structure_determination.topic: Matching the detection method to the question asked
detection_and_structure_determination.question: You know your product's structure and simply need the amount made in each of forty cultures. Which approach fits?

choices.A: NMR on each sample, integrating the diagnostic proton peaks
choices.B: Crystallography on each sample to confirm the structure first
choices.C: LCMS against an internal standard, reading the product peak
choices.D: A footprinting experiment on the biosynthetic gene cluster
choices.E: Size exclusion chromatography of each culture supernatant

detection_and_structure_determination.explanation: The structure is not in question, so the job is quantitation across many samples, which is what a chromatographic separation with a mass detector and a known standard does well and quickly. NMR needs milligrams of pure material per sample and crystallography needs a crystal, neither of which is practical forty times over, and the remaining methods answer entirely different questions.

detection_and_structure_determination.topic: Sequencing the methods for an unknown product
detection_and_structure_determination.question: A strain makes an unexpected compound of unknown structure. In what order would you characterize it?

choices.A: Crystallize it first, then purify it, then run NMR for the mass
choices.B: Run NMR on the crude extract, then purify what the spectrum shows
choices.C: Quantify it by LCMS first, then infer the structure from its retention
choices.D: Sequence the host genome, then predict the structure from the pathway
choices.E: Extract and purify it, get a mass, then solve the structure by NMR

detection_and_structure_determination.explanation: You need the compound clean before any structural method will work, and the cheapest structural information is the mass, which narrows the formula before you commit to a long experiment. NMR then builds the connectivity, with diffraction held in reserve for stereochemistry. A crude extract gives an uninterpretable spectrum, retention time identifies a known compound rather than describing an unknown one, and a predicted pathway is a hypothesis rather than a structure.

detection_and_structure_determination.topic: Distinguishing chromatographic separation from mass resolution
detection_and_structure_determination.question: Two isomers of identical formula co-elute on your column and the mass spectrometer reports one peak. What fixes it?

choices.A: A change in the chromatography, since their masses are identical
choices.B: An internal standard, which corrects for the overlapping signal
choices.C: A higher resolution mass analyzer, which will split the two
choices.D: A longer acquisition, which improves the counting statistics
choices.E: A UV detector in series, since isomers differ in absorbance

detection_and_structure_determination.explanation: Isomers have the same formula and therefore the same exact mass, so no amount of mass resolution will separate them; the discrimination has to come from the column, by changing the stationary phase, the gradient or the temperature until their retention times differ. Internal standards correct for ionization rather than for overlap, and longer acquisition sharpens a peak without splitting it.

activity_and_binding_assays.question: Purified alkaline phosphatase is given p-nitrophenyl phosphate and the tube turns yellow. What makes this the simple case?

choices.A: The enzyme is immobilized, so the product stays in one place
choices.B: The reaction itself produces a product you can read directly
choices.C: The substrate is radioactive, which makes detection sensitive
choices.D: A second enzyme converts the product to a colored species
choices.E: The enzyme is read by antibody rather than by its activity

activity_and_binding_assays.explanation: Hydrolysis releases p-nitrophenol, which is yellow, so the progress of the reaction is visible in the tube and can be read on a photometer without any further steps. Following the color over time at several substrate concentrations is what yields the kinetic parameters. A second enzyme in the readout is the coupled case, and antibody detection reports abundance rather than activity.

activity_and_binding_assays.topic: Distinguishing a coupled assay from a direct one
activity_and_binding_assays.question: What defines a coupled enzymatic assay?

choices.A: Two substrates are supplied to the enzyme at the same time
choices.B: The assay is run in both the forward and the reverse direction
choices.C: A second reaction converts the product into something readable
choices.D: The enzyme is assayed while still attached to the display host
choices.E: Two enzymes compete for the same substrate in one tube

activity_and_binding_assays.explanation: When the reaction of interest produces nothing you can see, you can sometimes attach a second, well-behaved reaction whose own readout is easy, so that the product of the first becomes the substrate of the second. The coupling is in the detection rather than in the chemistry being studied, and the reporting reaction has to be fast enough not to become the step you are measuring.

activity_and_binding_assays.topic: Knowing when a radioactive substrate is warranted
activity_and_binding_assays.question: Radioactive substrates are disfavored for their handling burden. Why are they still used?

choices.A: They report the stereochemistry of the product formed
choices.B: They work without purifying the enzyme beforehand
choices.C: They are the most sensitive way to follow a reaction run
choices.D: They avoid the need for any separation step at all
choices.E: They allow the reaction to be followed inside living cells

activity_and_binding_assays.explanation: A labeled substrate puts a signal on the reaction that can be counted at very low amounts, which remains the most sensitive way to watch a conversion that produces no color and little mass change. The cost is the radiation itself, with the licensing, waste handling and bureaucracy that goes with it, which is why the method is kept for cases that need the sensitivity.

activity_and_binding_assays.topic: Understanding what a filter binding assay separates
activity_and_binding_assays.question: A filter binding assay dispenses the reaction on TCA-soaked paper and washes repeatedly with TCA. What does that accomplish?

choices.A: It hydrolyzes the product so the label can be counted freely
choices.B: It retains precipitated macromolecules and washes small molecules away
choices.C: It separates the species by charge as they move through the paper
choices.D: It concentrates the sample by evaporating the aqueous solvent
choices.E: It quenches the enzyme so no further turnover can occur

activity_and_binding_assays.explanation: Acid precipitates macromolecules onto the filter while unincorporated small molecules, including free labeled amino acid, wash straight through. What stays on the paper is therefore label that became attached to something large, which after drying is counted by scintillation. Reading charged tRNA is the classic case, where nothing about the reaction changes color and the mass shift is one amino acid on a 76-mer.

activity_and_binding_assays.topic: Distinguishing a pulldown from an ELISA
activity_and_binding_assays.question: How does a pulldown differ from an ELISA in what it reports?

choices.A: A pulldown reports binding in real time without any label
choices.B: A pulldown maps where on a nucleic acid the protein binds
choices.C: A pulldown recovers the partner itself for further analysis
choices.D: A pulldown reports the dissociation constant of the pair
choices.E: A pulldown requires the antigen to be adsorbed to a plate

activity_and_binding_assays.explanation: A pulldown immobilizes a bait and captures whatever binds it from a mixture, and the point is that the captured partner comes off with it and can be run on a gel or identified by mass spectrometry. An ELISA asks whether and how much of a known partner is present through a layered colorimetric readout. Real-time label-free kinetics are what surface plasmon resonance provides, and footprinting is what locates a binding site.

activity_and_binding_assays.question: An ELISA immobilizes the antigen and then blocks the well with milk before anything else is added. Why?

choices.A: To supply the enzyme substrate that the final step requires
choices.B: To raise the local pH so the antibody will bind the antigen
choices.C: To cross-link the antigen so it cannot wash off the surface
choices.D: To occupy the remaining surface so later reagents cannot stick
choices.E: To remove antigen that failed to adsorb to the plastic surface

activity_and_binding_assays.explanation: Plastic adsorbs protein indiscriminately, so a well that has been coated with antigen still has bare surface that would bind the detection antibody and the conjugate directly and give signal with no specific binding at all. Flooding that surface with an irrelevant protein leaves the specific interaction as the only route to signal, which is why every well, including the controls, is blocked.

activity_and_binding_assays.topic: Reasoning about the layers of a sandwich readout
activity_and_binding_assays.question: An ELISA adds affibody, then a biotinylated anti-protein A antibody, then streptavidin-HRP, then peroxide and ABTS. What is the amplification?

choices.A: Each layer binds several of the layer beneath it, ending in turnover
choices.B: Each wash step concentrates the signal into a smaller volume
choices.C: The peroxide oxidizes the antigen, releasing many colored products
choices.D: The streptavidin binds four biotins, which is the whole of the gain
choices.E: The affibody is present in excess, which drives the binding forward

activity_and_binding_assays.explanation: Two things multiply. The stack is built so that each tier can engage more than one of the tier below, and the final tier carries an enzyme that keeps converting substrate for as long as the development runs. The biotin-streptavidin valency is one contribution rather than the whole of it, and nothing in the scheme oxidizes the antigen.

activity_and_binding_assays.topic: Knowing what surface plasmon resonance uniquely provides
activity_and_binding_assays.question: What does surface plasmon resonance give that an ELISA does not?

choices.A: A measurement made without purifying either binding partner
choices.B: The association and dissociation followed in real time, unlabeled
choices.C: Identification of an unknown partner from a complex mixture
choices.D: The position of the binding site on the immobilized partner
choices.E: A result that needs no immobilization of either partner

activity_and_binding_assays.explanation: Both methods immobilize one partner and flow the other over it, but plasmon resonance watches mass accumulate at the surface as it happens, so you see the binding phase and then the release when buffer replaces analyte, which gives rate constants rather than a single endpoint, and does so with no label on either partner. Identifying an unknown partner is what a pulldown is for.

activity_and_binding_assays.question: A footprinting experiment incubates end-labeled DNA with a protein, adds dilute DNase I, and runs the fragments on a gel. What is read out?

choices.A: Whether the protein binds the DNA at all under these conditions
choices.B: The dissociation constant of the protein for that DNA sequence
choices.C: How many protein molecules are bound to each DNA fragment
choices.D: The stretch the protein covered, seen as a gap in the ladder
choices.E: The rate at which the nuclease cuts the unprotected regions

activity_and_binding_assays.explanation: The protein shields the bases it sits on, so the nuclease cuts everywhere except there, and the fragment ladder on the gel shows a gap at the positions that were covered. The experiment answers where rather than whether, which is the distinction to keep: whether a protein is bound is a simpler question that a pulldown or a shift assay settles.

activity_and_binding_assays.topic: Matching an assay to what it must report
activity_and_binding_assays.question: You have a purified transcription factor and need to know which promoter region it occupies. Which experiment answers that?

choices.A: An ELISA against the factor, read colorimetrically on a plate
choices.B: A filter binding assay with a radiolabeled amino acid substrate
choices.C: Surface plasmon resonance with the factor flowed over the chip
choices.D: A footprinting experiment with a nuclease on labeled promoter DNA
choices.E: A sizing column to establish the factor's oligomeric state

activity_and_binding_assays.explanation: The question is positional, and footprinting is the method that returns a position. An ELISA quantifies the protein, plasmon resonance gives the kinetics of binding without saying where on the DNA it happens, and the sizing column characterizes the protein itself. The filter binding assay as described is set up for aminoacylation rather than for protein-DNA interaction at all.

cell_free_expression.topic: Knowing what a transcription-translation extract contains
cell_free_expression.question: What does a cell-free transcription-translation reaction supply?

choices.A: Intact cells permeabilized so that reagents can enter them
choices.B: Purified polymerase and ribosomes reconstituted from components
choices.C: A mixture of purified messenger RNA and amino acids only
choices.D: A cell lysate with the machinery, plus energy and nucleotides
choices.E: Membrane vesicles that carry out transcription internally

cell_free_expression.explanation: The usual extract is made by lysing cells and clearing the debris, which leaves the polymerase, ribosomes, transfer RNAs and factors in solution, and that lysate is then supplemented with an energy system, nucleotides and amino acids so synthesis can run. Fully reconstituted systems built from purified components do exist, but they are a different and much more expensive preparation.

cell_free_expression.question: Which step of a conventional characterization does a cell-free reaction let you skip?

choices.A: Sequencing the construct before it is tested
choices.B: Assembling the DNA that encodes the circuit
choices.C: Normalizing the readout against a reference
choices.D: Transforming the construct into a living host
choices.E: Measuring the output on an instrument afterward

cell_free_expression.explanation: You add DNA directly to the reaction, so there is no transformation, no outgrowth and no colony to pick, which is what compresses the turnaround from days to hours. Everything else still applies: the DNA has to be built and verified, and the output still has to be measured and normalized like any other assay.

cell_free_expression.topic: Understanding what removing the cell buys you
cell_free_expression.question: Testing a circuit in extract rather than in cells removes which complication?

choices.A: The need to supply an energy source for synthesis
choices.B: Growth, burden and native regulation acting on the circuit
choices.C: The requirement that the construct be sequence verified
choices.D: Variation between replicate reactions on the same day
choices.E: The dependence of the readout on the reporter chosen

cell_free_expression.explanation: In a living host the circuit competes for ribosomes, is affected by growth rate and stress, and sits inside native regulation that may act on its parts, all of which make a confusing result hard to attribute. An extract strips those away so the behavior you see is closer to the parts themselves. Energy must in fact be supplied deliberately, and replicate variation does not disappear.

cell_free_expression.topic: Rejecting claims cell-free does not support
cell_free_expression.question: Which claim about cell-free expression is not supported?

choices.A: It permits a construct to be tested without transformation
choices.B: It removes native regulation that would act on the circuit
choices.C: It shortens the time from DNA in hand to a measurement
choices.D: It allows reaction conditions to be set by the experimenter
choices.E: It produces higher protein yields than living cells do

cell_free_expression.explanation: Cell-free is convenient rather than productive: a living culture concentrates machinery and regenerates energy continuously, and extracts are often outperformed on yield per volume. The genuine advantages are speed, the absence of transformation, the removal of cellular regulation, and direct control of the reaction conditions, which is also what makes it useful for prototyping.

cell_free_expression.topic: Recognizing a control available only without cells
cell_free_expression.question: What can you set directly in an extract reaction that you cannot set in a cell?

choices.A: The concentration of each DNA template in the reaction
choices.B: The identity of the promoter driving the reporter gene
choices.C: The sequence of the ribosome binding site being tested
choices.D: The wavelength at which the reporter is read out
choices.E: The number of replicates included in the experiment

cell_free_expression.explanation: Template amount in a cell is set by copy number and by how the plasmid is maintained, neither of which you dial precisely, whereas in a reaction you pipette exactly how much of each template you want and can titrate one against another. The promoter, the ribosome binding site and the readout are design choices available in both formats.

cell_free_expression.topic: Reasoning about template form in an extract
cell_free_expression.question: Why can a PCR product be used directly as the template in many cell-free reactions?

choices.A: Because extracts replicate linear DNA before transcribing it
choices.B: Because no transformation or replication of the template is needed
choices.C: Because linear DNA is transcribed more efficiently than plasmid
choices.D: Because the reaction circularizes the fragment before expressing it
choices.E: Because exonucleases in the lysate stabilize the free ends

cell_free_expression.explanation: The template only has to be transcribed, not maintained, so it needs neither an origin nor a cell to live in, and a fragment straight off a PCR will do. That removes cloning from the loop entirely for a quick test. Extracts do not replicate or circularize the template, and exonucleases in the lysate degrade free ends rather than protecting them, which is why some systems add an inhibitor.

cell_free_expression.topic: Knowing the limits of a cell-free result
cell_free_expression.question: A circuit behaves as designed in extract. What does that not establish?

choices.A: That the parts can drive transcription and translation at all
choices.B: That the construct's sequence corresponds to the design
choices.C: That the reporter can be detected on your instrument
choices.D: That it will behave the same way inside a growing cell
choices.E: That the template was added at the intended concentration

cell_free_expression.explanation: The very thing an extract removes is the context the circuit will finally have to work in, so a clean result says the parts function while leaving open how they behave under burden, growth and native regulation. That is why cell-free is used for early triage and the promising designs are then moved into cells, rather than being treated as the final test.
