cell_free_expression.topic: Choosing between cell-free and whole-cell characterization
cell_free_expression.question: You must rank twenty candidate ribosome binding sites by tomorrow, with no cloned constructs yet. Which route fits?

choices.A: Transform each into cells and assay the colonies by plate reader
choices.B: Express each from a PCR product in extract and read the reporter
choices.C: Build a pooled library and sort the brightest cells by cytometry
choices.D: Assay each in cells and confirm the ranking by cycle sequencing
choices.E: Purify the reporter from each and quantify it by mass spectrometry

cell_free_expression.explanation: The constraint is time and the absence of clones, and adding PCR products straight to reactions skips cloning, transformation and outgrowth, which are the days you do not have. Every route through living cells needs transformation first, pooling answers a different question than ranking twenty defined candidates, and purifying each reporter is far heavier than the question requires.

cell_free_expression.topic: Knowing how an extract is made
cell_free_expression.question: How is a transcription-translation extract typically prepared?

choices.A: Cells are grown, lysed, and the debris cleared by centrifugation
choices.B: Each component is purified separately and then recombined
choices.C: Cells are permeabilized with detergent and used whole
choices.D: Ribosomes are isolated on a sucrose gradient and used alone
choices.E: Spent culture medium is concentrated and then buffered

cell_free_expression.explanation: Growing cells in mid-exponential phase, breaking them open, and spinning out the membranes and debris leaves a soluble fraction containing the machinery of expression, which is then supplemented and often dialyzed. Reconstitution from purified parts gives a cleaner but costlier system, and the remaining options would leave out the ribosomes, the factors, or both.

cell_free_expression.topic: Diagnosing a reaction that produces nothing
cell_free_expression.question: A construct gives no reporter in extract while a known-good control template works in the same batch. What does that indicate?

choices.A: The extract has lost activity and should be replaced
choices.B: The energy system has been exhausted during the reaction
choices.C: The problem lies with that construct rather than the reaction
choices.D: The reporter cannot be detected at the chosen wavelength
choices.E: The template concentration was too high and inhibited synthesis

cell_free_expression.explanation: That is what the control template is in the reaction for. Since it expressed in the same batch, under the same energy system and read on the same instrument, the machinery, the reagents and the detection are all working, which localizes the failure to the construct itself: its sequence, its parts, or how much of it was added.

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.question: What makes a cluster on an Illumina flow cell bright enough to read?

choices.A: Each fragment is amplified in place into a clonal patch
choices.B: Each fragment carries many dye molecules along its length
choices.C: The polymerase incorporates several labeled bases per cycle
choices.D: The flow cell is coated in a fluorophore that the base displaces
choices.E: Each fragment is read many times over in successive passes

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.explanation: A single molecule does not give enough signal to photograph, so every bound fragment is amplified where it sits into a small patch of identical copies that all add one base at the same time. The chemistry then allows exactly one base per cycle, carrying both a dye and a blocking group, so each patch gives one color per cycle across a few hundred cycles.

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.question: Why does each Illumina cycle add exactly one base, even though all four are present?

choices.A: Each base carries a blocking group that stops further addition
choices.B: Only one base is complementary at any given position
choices.C: The polymerase is inactivated after each incorporation event
choices.D: The wash step removes the polymerase between additions
choices.E: The camera exposure is short enough to catch only one base

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.explanation: All four bases are supplied together, each with a dye and a reversible blocking group, so whichever one is incorporated terminates the extension until the block is chemically stripped. That is what keeps the patches in step with one another: wash, photograph the whole surface, strip the dye and the block, and go again. Complementarity decides which base goes in, not how many.

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.topic: Reasoning about what a read length preserves
choosing_a_sequencing_platform.question: Your library's variants differ at positions spread across 1.2 kb of a gene, and you need to know which differences occur together. What does that require?

choices.A: Deeper coverage on a short-read instrument than usual
choices.B: Paired-end rather than single-end short reads
choices.C: Reads long enough to span the gene on one molecule
choices.D: A larger number of total reads from the same instrument
choices.E: A shorter amplicon spanning only the variable positions

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.explanation: Which differences travel together is a property of a single molecule, and a short read sees only a fragment of each one, so it reports which variants exist without saying how they are combined. Only a read covering the whole gene keeps that linkage intact. More depth and more reads give better counting of the same fragmentary information, and paired ends extend the span only a little.

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.topic: Choosing short reads for a counting problem
choosing_a_sequencing_platform.question: You need to count how often each of a million short barcodes appears in a pool. Why is a short-read instrument the right choice?

choices.A: Because short reads are more accurate per base than long reads
choices.B: Because it returns enough reads to count every barcode deeply
choices.C: Because only short-read chemistry can resolve a barcode at all
choices.D: Because barcodes cannot be read by a nanopore instrument
choices.E: Because short reads preserve linkage across the construct

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.explanation: The barcode is short, so read length is not the constraint; what matters is how many reads you get, and a short-read run returns them in the billions at the lowest cost per read, which is what deep counting requires. Long-read instruments return millions rather than billions. Raw accuracy on nanopore is now around 99.75 percent, so calling barcodes is no longer the objection it once was.

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.question: What is measured as DNA passes through a nanopore, and what controls the speed?

choices.A: Fluorescence from each base, with the voltage setting the speed
choices.B: Mass of each nucleotide, with a pump controlling the flow rate
choices.C: Current through the pore, with a motor protein ratcheting the strand
choices.D: Current through the pore, with the voltage alone setting the speed
choices.E: Light scattered by the strand, with a motor feeding it through

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.explanation: A voltage drives the strand through the pore and the ionic current changes according to what is occupying the narrow part of it, which is read as sequence. On its own the field pulls the DNA through far too fast to measure, so a motor protein at the mouth of the pore feeds the strand a step at a time, which is what turns a translocation into a read.

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.topic: Reasoning about what the pore current reports
choosing_a_sequencing_platform.question: Why does the current level in a nanopore not correspond to a single base?

choices.A: Because the motor protein advances the strand by several bases
choices.B: Because the dye on each base takes time to be stripped away
choices.C: Because the current is averaged over the whole read for accuracy
choices.D: Because both strands of the duplex pass through together
choices.E: Because several bases occupy the narrow constriction at once

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.explanation: A stretch of the strand sits in the constriction at any moment, so the measured level is a function of several neighboring bases rather than of one, and the sequence has to be inferred from the series of levels rather than read off them directly. That is why basecalling is a model-fitting problem on this platform, and why its accuracy improved so much as the models did.

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.question: Where do PacBio HiFi and nanopore sit relative to a short-read instrument?

choices.A: They give more reads, which makes them better for counting
choices.B: They give shorter reads at higher accuracy per base
choices.C: They are the only platforms that can read a barcode reliably
choices.D: They give long reads at millions, not billions, of reads
choices.E: They read DNA without any amplification of the library

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.explanation: Both long-read platforms deliver reads in the tens of thousands of bases, with HiFi mode calling about ninety percent of bases at Q30 or better, but they return millions of reads per cell rather than billions. That pairing is what decides their use: they are the answer when a whole variant must stay on one molecule, and the wrong answer when the job is deep counting of short features.

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.question: Which statement about platform availability is correct?

choices.A: Ion Torrent was retired in 2016 and 454 remains on sale
choices.B: Both 454 and Ion Torrent were retired in the same year
choices.C: Nanopore was withdrawn once accuracy objections were raised
choices.D: HiSeq remains the current Illumina production instrument
choices.E: 454 was retired in 2016; Ion Torrent is still sold

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.explanation: Roche announced the end of 454 in 2013 and stopped supporting it by mid-2016, while Ion Torrent is still sold and remains distinctive for detecting incorporation semiconductor-electrically rather than optically. Illumina retired HiSeq in 2024 in favor of newer instruments, and nanopore is very much current, with its accuracy objection largely answered.

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.topic: Choosing a method for a single isolate
choosing_a_sequencing_platform.question: You have picked one colony and want to confirm the construct it carries. Which method fits, and why?

choices.A: Short-read sequencing, since it gives the deepest coverage
choices.B: Nanopore, since only long reads span a whole plasmid
choices.C: Cycle sequencing, since the sample is a single clonal template
choices.D: Digital droplet PCR, since it counts molecules precisely
choices.E: Paired-end sequencing, since both strands must be read

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.explanation: One colony is one sequence, so there is nothing to deconvolute and no counting to do: an ordinary cycle sequencing reaction on the purified plasmid reads it directly and cheaply. The massively parallel platforms exist to read many different molecules at once, which is effort and expense wasted on a single clonal template, and droplet PCR counts rather than sequences.

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.topic: Reasoning about what a platform choice costs
choosing_a_sequencing_platform.question: Why is cost per read, rather than cost per base, the figure that matters for a barcode counting experiment?

choices.A: Because reads are priced individually by the sequencing provider
choices.B: Because each barcode needs one read regardless of read length
choices.C: Because longer reads cost less per base than shorter ones do
choices.D: Because the instrument charges by run rather than by sample
choices.E: Because barcode reads are shorter than the instrument minimum

choosing_a_sequencing_platform.explanation: Counting is a matter of how many observations you collect, and each observation of a barcode consumes one read whatever that read's length. Paying for a platform that reads twenty thousand bases per read buys length you throw away while limiting how many observations you can afford, which is precisely the mismatch between a long-read instrument and a counting problem.

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.question: Why attach a barcode to each member of a library rather than reading the variant region itself?

choices.A: Because the variant region cannot be amplified by any primer pair
choices.B: Because a short fixed-position tag is cheap and uniform to read
choices.C: Because barcodes are more accurate per base than variant sequence
choices.D: Because the barcode protects the variant region from degradation
choices.E: Because sequencing a coding region requires a long-read platform

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.explanation: A barcode turns reading the identity of a variant into reading a short sequence that sits in a known place and is the same length for everyone, which is cheap, uniform and easy to count. The variants themselves may differ in length and in sequence context, which is exactly what makes reading them directly awkward and biased.

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.topic: Choosing a barcode length from the diversity needed
counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.question: Roughly how long must a barcode be to label a library of about a billion members?

choices.A: About 15 bases, since 4^15 is on the order of 10^9
choices.B: About 9 bases, since 9 x 4 is close to 10^9
choices.C: About 30 bases, since each base labels two members
choices.D: About 20 bases, since 20^4 is on the order of 10^9
choices.E: About 5 bases, since 4^5 covers a billion sequences

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.explanation: The number of distinct barcodes is four raised to the length, so a billion needs about fifteen bases because four to the fifteenth is around a billion. This is the same product-across-positions arithmetic as library diversity, applied to a tag rather than to a design. Multiplying the length by four, or raising the length to the fourth power, both invert the roles of base count and position count.

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.topic: Understanding why the barcode is placed apart from the variant
counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.question: Why is the barcode put somewhere other than inside the sequence being characterized, with a priming site between them?

choices.A: So the barcode is transcribed while the variant region is not
choices.B: So that the barcode can be read without sequencing the variant
choices.C: So every amplicon has the same length and sequence context
choices.D: So the variant region is shielded from polymerase errors
choices.E: So the barcode can be removed before the library is cloned

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.explanation: If the genes differ in length or in flanking sequence you cannot amplify them all evenly, and unequal amplification corrupts the counts. Putting a standard priming site between the barcode and the gene means the product you sequence has the same length and much the same sequence whatever variant it came from, so what you count reflects abundance rather than how well each one amplified.

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.topic: Explaining the variable-length spacer in the construct
counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.question: An Illumina amplicon for a multiplex experiment carries a variable-length spacer before the region of interest. What is it for?

choices.A: To standardize the total length of every amplicon in the pool
choices.B: To create sequence diversity in the early cycles of the run
choices.C: To provide a second priming site for the reverse read
choices.D: To separate the two adapters by a defined distance
choices.E: To act as a second barcode identifying the sample

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.explanation: A multiplex library is largely the same sequence in every molecule, and a flow cell reading identical bases across the whole surface at once calls them badly. Staggering where each molecule starts by inserting a random-length spacer restores base diversity in those early cycles, which is a technicality of the instrument rather than anything to do with the biology.

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.topic: Recognizing the limits of a raw read count
counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.question: A variant accounts for five percent of the reads from a pool. What does that number tell you on its own?

choices.A: That the variant is five percent more active than average
choices.B: That five percent of cells carried that variant originally
choices.C: That the variant makes up five percent of this pool, no more
choices.D: That the variant was enriched fivefold during the experiment
choices.E: That the variant's expression is five percent of the maximum

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.explanation: A read fraction is a composition of the sample you sequenced, and nothing else. Turning it into a measurement needs a denominator: the same variant's share in the input, in the DNA, or in an earlier round. Without that comparison a large share may reflect how well the variant clones or amplifies rather than anything about its function, which is the lesson the SELEX data makes.

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.topic: Identifying the denominator in a barcoded expression experiment
counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.question: In CRE-Seq, barcode frequencies in the mRNA pool are divided by what, and why?

choices.A: By the total read count, to correct for run-to-run depth
choices.B: By the frequency of a spiked-in synthetic control barcode
choices.C: By their frequencies in the DNA of the same input sample
choices.D: By the barcode frequencies measured in an uninduced control
choices.E: By the length of each promoter element being characterized

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.explanation: Each variant is present in the transfected population at its own abundance, so a barcode can be common in the message simply because its construct was common in the DNA. Sequencing the input DNA gives each barcode's starting share, and dividing message by DNA converts an abundance into an expression level per construct. Total depth is handled by working in frequencies throughout.

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.topic: Being precise about what RNA-seq measures
counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.question: What does an RNA-seq read count for a gene actually report?

choices.A: The activity of that gene's promoter in the sampled cells
choices.B: The absolute number of transcripts per cell in the sample
choices.C: The rate at which that gene is being transcribed per minute
choices.D: The steady-state message share, transcription and decay together
choices.E: The amount of protein produced from that gene in the sample

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.explanation: You are measuring how much message is present at the moment of extraction, which is set by synthesis and degradation together rather than by transcription alone, and you are measuring it as a share of everything else in the same sample because total reads are set by the instrument. That is why these experiments are framed as one condition against another rather than as absolute quantities.

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.topic: Comparing counts between rounds rather than reading an endpoint
counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.question: Why are selection experiments read by comparing counts between rounds rather than by ranking the final pool?

choices.A: Because the final round contains too few reads to rank reliably
choices.B: Because sequencing error accumulates across successive rounds
choices.C: Because a rising share, not a large share, shows selection acting
choices.D: Because the earlier rounds are more diverse and so more informative
choices.E: Because the final pool is dominated by the input library

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.explanation: Abundance at the end has no reference point, and a sequence can be plentiful because it synthesizes and amplifies well. A trajectory across rounds supplies the before, so what you report is how much each sequence grew. In the published case the ten most abundant sequences were the same in every round and showed no enrichment, while the real hits started rare and climbed by thousands of fold.

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.topic: Understanding what makes droplet PCR digital
counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.question: Why is digital droplet PCR described as digital?

choices.A: The amplification curve is read digitally rather than on film
choices.B: Each droplet scores positive or negative, and droplets are counted
choices.C: The instrument reports copy number as a binary representation
choices.D: The reaction is cycled digitally without a thermal gradient
choices.E: Each droplet is sequenced to determine what it contained

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.explanation: The sample is diluted until most droplets receive either one template or none, so after cycling each droplet is simply yes or no, and the concentration follows from counting how many were positive. That replaces comparing an amplification curve against a standard curve with direct counting. Putting a primer-coated bead in each droplet turns the same partitioning into clonal amplification on beads.

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.topic: Choosing the right denominator for a pooled measurement
counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.question: A pooled library of ribosome binding sites is read by counting barcoded transcripts. What must be measured alongside?

choices.A: The growth rate of the pooled culture during the experiment
choices.B: The total number of reads returned by the sequencing run
choices.C: The barcode composition of the DNA going into the experiment
choices.D: The fluorescence of the pool measured on a plate reader
choices.E: The length of each barcode in the designed library

counting_barcodes_and_normalizing.explanation: Transcript counts per barcode are meaningless until divided by how much of that construct was present to be transcribed, so the input DNA has to be sequenced as its own sample. That denominator absorbs uneven representation from the cloning and the transformation, leaving a per-construct expression level. Total reads cancel once everything is expressed as frequencies.

designing_a_library_readout.topic: Listing what a molecule needs to be read on an instrument
designing_a_library_readout.question: What must be present on a molecule before it can be read in a pooled Illumina experiment?

choices.A: A barcode and a selectable marker for the host strain
choices.B: An origin of replication and a promoter for the insert
choices.C: A polyadenylation signal at the 3' end of the construct
choices.D: A restriction site flanking each end of the variable region
choices.E: The adapters and primer binding sites the instrument needs

designing_a_library_readout.explanation: The flow cell binds molecules through defined adapter sequences and the sequencing primers anneal to fixed sites inside them, so a fragment without that architecture is simply not read. Markers, origins and promoters matter for propagating and expressing the library in cells, and restriction sites are a construction convenience rather than an instrument requirement.

designing_a_library_readout.topic: Checking that the informative region falls within the read
designing_a_library_readout.question: Your variable region sits 400 bases from the sequencing primer and the run gives 150 base reads. What happens?

choices.A: The read covers the region at reduced accuracy near its end
choices.B: The instrument extends the read automatically to reach it
choices.C: The read stops well short, so the region is never seen
choices.D: The paired read from the other end compensates for the gap
choices.E: The region is recovered by assembling overlapping reads

designing_a_library_readout.explanation: Reading begins at the primer site and runs for as many cycles as the run was configured for, so anything beyond that distance is never visited. The layout has to put the informative region within the read length of a priming site, which is a design decision made before the library is built rather than something recoverable afterward. Paired ends read inward from the other adapter and do not bridge an arbitrary gap.

designing_a_library_readout.topic: Knowing when a barcode is necessary
designing_a_library_readout.question: In which case must the construct carry a barcode rather than being identified by its own sequence?

choices.A: When the variants differ only in a region outside the read
choices.B: When the variants differ by single substitutions across a gene
choices.C: When the library contains more members than can be transformed
choices.D: When the readout is fluorescence rather than sequencing
choices.E: When the variants are all of exactly the same length

designing_a_library_readout.explanation: If what distinguishes the variants cannot be reached by the read, nothing about the molecule you sequence identifies it, so a tag has to be placed where the read can see it and associated with the variant once, by long reads or by clone-by-clone sequencing. Variants differing within the read can be told apart directly, and being the same length is a convenience rather than a reason.

designing_a_library_readout.topic: Linking a barcode to the variant it labels
designing_a_library_readout.question: You have barcoded a library of gene-length variants. How is each barcode associated with the variant it tags?

choices.A: By the order in which the barcodes were synthesized
choices.B: By sequencing barcode and variant together on long reads
choices.C: By the position of the barcode within the construct
choices.D: By counting how often each barcode appears in the pool
choices.E: By designing each barcode to encode its variant's sequence

designing_a_library_readout.explanation: A barcode means nothing until you know what it labels, and establishing that requires reading the tag and the variant on the same molecule, which is a long-read job done once for the library. After that the cheap short-read counting runs can read barcodes alone. Counting frequencies measures abundance rather than identity, and a fifteen-base tag cannot encode a gene.

designing_a_library_readout.topic: Recognizing amplification bias in a pooled readout
designing_a_library_readout.question: Why does amplifying variants that differ in length distort the counts?

choices.A: Because longer products carry more polymerase errors per molecule
choices.B: Because length changes which adapters can ligate to the ends
choices.C: Because longer products bind the flow cell more readily
choices.D: Because shorter products are lost during the cleanup steps
choices.E: Because shorter products amplify more efficiently in the same reaction

designing_a_library_readout.explanation: In a shared reaction the shorter template finishes extension sooner and competes better cycle after cycle, so its share of the product grows relative to the longer one regardless of how abundant each was to begin with. The counts then report amplification rather than composition, which is why the readout is designed so that every amplicon is the same length.

designing_a_library_readout.topic: Judging whether a proposed library can be decoded
designing_a_library_readout.question: A proposal barcodes a promoter library but places the barcode on the plasmid outside the transcript. Can expression be read?

choices.A: Yes, since the barcode still identifies the construct in the DNA
choices.B: Yes, provided the plasmid is sequenced alongside the messages
choices.C: No, since the barcode must appear in the message to be counted
choices.D: No, since barcodes cannot be placed outside a coding sequence
choices.E: Yes, if the barcode is read by long-read sequencing instead

designing_a_library_readout.explanation: The readout counts messages, so the tag has to be transcribed along with the reporter in order to appear in the pool you sequence. A barcode present only in the plasmid identifies constructs in the DNA sample, which is the denominator, and leaves the numerator with nothing to count. Placing the barcode in the transcribed region, downstream of the reporter, is the fix.

designing_a_library_readout.topic: Designing a readout that records positions
designing_a_library_readout.question: A probing experiment must record, for each molecule, where reverse transcription stopped. What makes that countable?

choices.A: A barcode identifying which RNA each cDNA came from
choices.B: A long read spanning the whole of every RNA in the pool
choices.C: An adapter ligated to the cDNA 3' end, fixing the stop position
choices.D: A fluorescent label on the reverse transcription primer
choices.E: A restriction digest that cuts at every stop position

designing_a_library_readout.explanation: The information is in where the enzyme fell off, so the end created by that event has to be captured and turned into something a sequencer can locate. Ligating an adapter to the new 3' end makes every truncated product amplifiable and puts the stop position at a defined distance from a priming site, so counting reads by length reports the distribution of stops.

designing_a_library_readout.topic: Reasoning about reads required per library member
designing_a_library_readout.question: A library has 10^5 members and you want about 100 reads each. Which expression gives the reads needed?

choices.A: 10^5 x 100, the members times the reads wanted each
choices.B: 10^5 / 100, the members divided by the depth wanted
choices.C: 100^5, the depth raised to the member count
choices.D: 10^5 + 100, the members plus the depth wanted
choices.E: 4^15, the number of barcodes the library requires

designing_a_library_readout.explanation: Depth per member times the number of members gives the total observations required, so a hundred reads each across a hundred thousand members needs about ten million reads, which is comfortably within one short-read run. Doing the arithmetic before the run is what tells you whether the experiment fits on the instrument and how much of a run to buy.

designing_a_library_readout.topic: Accounting for uneven representation when choosing depth
designing_a_library_readout.question: Your library is known to be skewed, with some members tenfold rarer than the mean. How does that affect the sequencing depth?

choices.A: It does not, since depth is set by the member count alone
choices.B: It lowers the requirement, since fewer members are present
choices.C: It makes the experiment impossible to interpret at any depth
choices.D: It raises it only if the skew lies within the barcode region
choices.E: It raises it, since the rarest members set the depth needed

designing_a_library_readout.explanation: Average depth is not what limits the result; the members you are most likely to miss or to count badly are the rare ones, so the run has to be deep enough that even those receive enough reads to be measured. This is the same reasoning as coverage in library construction, where uniform sampling is assumed and skew forces you to sample deeper.

designing_a_library_readout.topic: Sequencing the design decisions for a pooled readout
designing_a_library_readout.question: In what order should a pooled characterization be designed?

choices.A: Build the library, then choose a platform that can read it
choices.B: Choose the platform, then design the layout the question needs
choices.C: Decide what must be read together, then pick platform, then layout
choices.D: Design the layout first, then decide what the question requires
choices.E: Sequence a pilot pool, then decide what the readout should be

designing_a_library_readout.explanation: The question dictates what has to stay on one molecule and what merely has to be counted, which decides the platform, which in turn fixes the read length and so the layout of adapters, barcode and informative region. Building first and shopping for an instrument afterward is how libraries end up undecodable, since no run can recover linkage the construct never preserved.

why_automate.question: A workflow that was run by hand is moved onto a liquid handler. What happens to the controls it needed?

choices.A: They are still required, since automation changes execution only
choices.B: They can be dropped, since the instrument transfers consistently
choices.C: They are replaced by the instrument's own calibration records
choices.D: They need only be run once, when the method is first validated
choices.E: They become unnecessary once the run log shows no errors

why_automate.explanation: Controls exist to tell you whether the biology and the reagents behaved, and a machine making the transfers does not speak to either. What automation removes is variability in how the steps were carried out, which is a different source of error from the ones a control detects. Calibration records and run logs attest to the instrument rather than to the experiment.

why_automate.question: In what sense does automation improve reproducibility?

choices.A: It eliminates biological variation between replicate cultures
choices.B: It standardizes the reagents supplied by the manufacturer
choices.C: It removes the need to repeat an experiment at all
choices.D: It makes every result statistically significant by design
choices.E: The same operations are performed the same way every run

why_automate.explanation: A liquid handler executing a written protocol makes the same transfers in the same order with the same timing, which removes the day-to-day and person-to-person drift that makes manual work hard to repeat. The biology still varies, replicates are still required, and significance comes from the design and the data rather than from the instrument.

why_automate.question: A lab automates a workflow that it only runs a few times a year. What justifies that?

choices.A: Throughput, since the instrument runs faster than a person
choices.B: Cost, since instrument time is cheaper than technician time
choices.C: Nothing, since automation pays only at high throughput
choices.D: Correctness and reproducibility, which matter at any scale
choices.E: Reduced reagent consumption on every individual run

why_automate.explanation: Throughput is only one of the reasons and it is the one that needs volume to pay off. Getting the procedure right, having it recorded exactly, and being able to check it before it runs are worth having whether you execute it twice or two thousand times, and for a rarely run but intricate protocol they are often the whole justification.

why_automate.question: Which claim about automating an experiment is not supportable?

choices.A: It records exactly which operations were performed
choices.B: It allows a protocol to be simulated before execution
choices.C: It performs transfers more consistently than a person
choices.D: It scales a workflow to many more samples at once
choices.E: It assures that the resulting construct will function

why_automate.explanation: Whether a construct works is a question about biology, and executing a flawed design perfectly produces a perfectly executed flawed design. What automation delivers is faithful execution, a record of it, the chance to check the plan in advance, and scale. Confusing careful execution with a guarantee of success is the error to avoid.

why_automate.question: What does simulating a construction file actually verify?

choices.A: That the designed product follows from the stated operations
choices.B: That the enzymes in the protocol are still active in the freezer
choices.C: That the final construct will express at the intended level
choices.D: That the transformation will yield sufficient colonies
choices.E: That the oligos were synthesized without any errors

why_automate.explanation: The simulation applies each operation to the sequences as written and reports what comes out, so it catches a primer that anneals in the wrong place, a digest with an unintended site, or a product that is not what the file claims. It says nothing about reagent quality, about how the construct behaves in a cell, or about what the synthesizer actually delivered.

why_automate.question: Why is the record of what an automated run performed valuable even when the run succeeds?

choices.A: Because it can be submitted in place of a laboratory notebook
choices.B: Because it is required before results may be published
choices.C: Because it establishes which operator is responsible
choices.D: Because it proves the reagents were within their shelf life
choices.E: Because it allows the run to be repeated or diagnosed exactly

why_automate.explanation: A successful run you cannot reconstruct is a result you cannot build on. An exact record lets the same procedure be executed again months later, lets a later failure be compared against what worked, and lets someone else run it without relearning the details. That is the same argument as writing a construction file rather than describing the cloning in prose.

why_automate.question: How does automation change which library sizes can be screened clone by clone?

choices.A: It removes the need for genotype-phenotype linkage in a pool
choices.B: It makes selections unnecessary for libraries of any scale
choices.C: It allows libraries of any size to be screened individually
choices.D: It raises the practical ceiling from hundreds into the thousands
choices.E: It lowers the coverage a library must be built to

why_automate.explanation: Picking and assaying by hand tops out in the hundreds, and a colony picker with plate handling moves that into the thousands or tens of thousands, which is a real extension of the arrayed regime. It does not reach the millions, so the largest libraries still require pooled selections, and nothing about automation changes the coverage a design demands.

why_automate.topic: Distinguishing errors automation prevents from those it does not
why_automate.question: Which failure would automation most plausibly have prevented?

choices.A: A promoter that proves weaker in the host than expected
choices.B: A library skewed by bias in the degenerate phosphoramidite mix
choices.C: A toxic gene product that slows the growth of the culture
choices.D: A plasmid lost from the population during outgrowth
choices.E: Two samples swapped between wells during a manual transfer

why_automate.explanation: Automation addresses execution errors: transfers made in the wrong order, to the wrong well, or at the wrong volume, and the barcoding and tracking that go with it make a swap both less likely and discoverable afterward. Promoter strength, synthesis bias, toxicity and plasmid loss are all properties of the chemistry or the biology that execute faithfully whatever you do.

why_automate.topic: Recognizing when automation is not warranted
why_automate.question: When is writing and validating an automated protocol not worth it?

choices.A: When the procedure will be repeated many times over months
choices.B: When the procedure is intricate and easy to get wrong by hand
choices.C: When the run must be documented precisely for later repetition
choices.D: When a handful of samples are handled once and never again
choices.E: When the sample count exceeds what a person can pipette

why_automate.explanation: Automating has its own cost in method development and validation, which is repaid by repetition, by intricacy, or by scale. A one-off handful of samples offers none of those, so the honest answer is to pipette them. The other situations are the cases where the investment pays, which is why they are the standard arguments for automating.

why_automate.topic: Reasoning about where verification sits in the workflow
why_automate.question: Why is it valuable that a design can be checked before any reagent is consumed?

choices.A: Because reagents degrade once a protocol has begun running
choices.B: Because a failure found at the bench costs days and materials
choices.C: Because simulated constructs need not be sequence verified
choices.D: Because errors found later cannot be corrected in the design
choices.E: Because checking afterward requires sequencing every clone

why_automate.explanation: A design error discovered after cloning has already cost the oligos, the enzymes, the transformations and the week spent on them, and it still has to be fixed and run again. Catching the same error in a simulation costs minutes. Errors found later can of course be corrected, which is precisely why the comparison is about cost rather than about possibility.

laboratory_instruments.topic: Knowing how acoustic droplet ejection works
laboratory_instruments.question: What is distinctive about how an acoustic droplet ejection instrument transfers liquid?

choices.A: It uses sound to eject nanoliter droplets with no contact
choices.B: It uses disposable tips to transfer microliter volumes
choices.C: It uses a vacuum manifold to draw liquid between plates
choices.D: It uses positive displacement through a fixed steel needle
choices.E: It uses capillary action along a coated glass filament

laboratory_instruments.explanation: A focused acoustic pulse from beneath the source well throws a precisely sized droplet upward into a plate held above it, so nothing touches the liquid and there are no tips to change or wash. That is what makes it the answer when the volumes are in nanoliters and carryover between samples must be impossible.

laboratory_instruments.question: What is a tip-based liquid handler best suited to?

choices.A: Contactless transfer of nanoliter volumes between plates
choices.B: Microliter transfers across plates, with tips changed between
choices.C: Picking individual colonies from an agar plate into wells
choices.D: Sealing plates so that cultures do not evaporate overnight
choices.E: Reading absorbance and fluorescence from a plate of samples

laboratory_instruments.explanation: A tip-based machine is the workhorse for the microliter regime: aspirating and dispensing reagents and samples around plates, with fresh tips wherever carryover matters. It cannot reach nanoliter accuracy reliably and it does not touch solid colonies. The other options describe the colony picker, the plate sealer and the plate reader.

laboratory_instruments.topic: Knowing what a colony picker does
laboratory_instruments.question: What does a colony picker with image recognition contribute to a screening workflow?

choices.A: It transfers nanoliter volumes between source and destination
choices.B: It sorts cells by fluorescence into separate collection tubes
choices.C: It seals and barcodes the plates once they have been filled
choices.D: It reads the fluorescence of each colony while on the plate
choices.E: It arrays individual colonies from plates into microtiter wells

laboratory_instruments.explanation: The picker images the plate, identifies discrete colonies, and moves each into its own well, which is the step that converts a plate of thousands of clones into an addressable array that the rest of the automation can handle. It is what makes arrayed screening of thousands feasible; sorting a pooled population by fluorescence is a cytometer's job.

laboratory_instruments.topic: Reasoning about why contactless transfer is needed
laboratory_instruments.question: A screen requires 25 nanoliters of each of forty reagents into every well of many plates. Why is tip-based transfer the wrong tool?

choices.A: Tips cannot be changed quickly enough between the transfers
choices.B: Tips are below their accurate range and would be consumed in thousands
choices.C: Tips cannot aspirate from a plate, only from a trough reservoir
choices.D: Tips would dilute the reagents by retaining buffer internally
choices.E: Tips cannot reach the bottom of a 384-well plate reliably

laboratory_instruments.explanation: Two things fail at once. Twenty-five nanoliters sits well below the volume a disposable tip dispenses accurately, and forty reagents across many plates means tens of thousands of tip changes if carryover is to be avoided. Contactless acoustic transfer answers both, since the droplet is ejected by sound from the source well and nothing is dipped into the liquid at all.

laboratory_instruments.question: What does a microfluidic device offer that a plate-based workflow does not?

choices.A: Reactions in very small volumes, often compartmentalized
choices.B: Higher reagent volumes per reaction for better precision
choices.C: The ability to pick and array individual colonies
choices.D: Direct sequencing of the samples it processes
choices.E: Barcoded tracking of each sample through the workflow

laboratory_instruments.explanation: Channels and droplets let reactions run in volumes far below a well, which saves reagent and, when each droplet is its own compartment, keeps a template with whatever it produces. That compartmentalization is what makes microfluidics a route to genotype-phenotype linkage as well as a way to miniaturize. Tracking and picking belong to other parts of the automation.

laboratory_instruments.topic: Understanding sample tracking in an automated lab
laboratory_instruments.question: What problem does putting a two-dimensional barcode on every tube solve?

choices.A: It identifies which library member each tube contains
choices.B: It allows the tube's contents to be sequenced without opening it
choices.C: It records which samples went where across a long workflow
choices.D: It prevents evaporation from the tube during storage
choices.E: It replaces the need to label plates with their contents

laboratory_instruments.explanation: As soon as samples move through many plates and many steps, the hardest thing to maintain is the mapping between a physical position and what is supposed to be in it. A machine-readable code on each tube lets every transfer be recorded against identity rather than against a position someone wrote down, which is what makes a swap discoverable. It does not know what is inside the tube, only which tube it is.

laboratory_instruments.topic: Knowing what a plate sealer is for
laboratory_instruments.question: Why is a plate sealer part of an automated culture workflow?

choices.A: It sterilizes the plate surface before the cultures are added
choices.B: It arrays the colonies into the wells of a fresh plate
choices.C: It mixes the wells by applying pressure across the plate
choices.D: It normalizes the volume in every well of the plate
choices.E: It applies a film so cultures do not evaporate or cross-contaminate

laboratory_instruments.explanation: Small culture volumes in a warm incubator evaporate quickly, and the edge wells go first, which is one of the commonest sources of a spurious pattern across a plate. A sealing film holds the volume and keeps wells from splashing into one another, while still allowing gas exchange in the breathable versions used for growth.

laboratory_instruments.topic: Recognizing an instrument applied to the wrong job
laboratory_instruments.question: A proposal picks the brightest clones from a million-colony plate using a colony picker. What is wrong?

choices.A: A picker cannot distinguish colonies from one another at all
choices.B: A picker transfers liquid rather than solid colony material
choices.C: A picker cannot array into plates without a liquid handler
choices.D: A picker arrays thousands, far short of a million colonies
choices.E: A picker requires the colonies to be fluorescent to find them

laboratory_instruments.explanation: The instrument is capable of what it does but not at this scale: arraying into 96-well or 384-well plates puts a ceiling in the thousands or tens of thousands, and a million colonies would need thousands of plates. A library this size has to be enriched first, by scraping and sorting, before any clone is arrayed and grown.

laboratory_instruments.topic: Matching the instrument to the kind of sample
laboratory_instruments.question: Which instrument handles a solid sample rather than a liquid one?

choices.A: The acoustic dispenser, which ejects droplets upward
choices.B: The plate reader, which illuminates the well contents
choices.C: The plate washer, which aspirates and refills wells
choices.D: The tip-based handler, which aspirates from a reservoir
choices.E: The colony picker, which lifts cells from agar

laboratory_instruments.explanation: Everything else in a typical automation stack moves or measures liquid, and the colony picker is the one that engages with cells growing on a solid surface, lifting material from a chosen colony into a well of medium. That is why it sits at the boundary between plating and the liquid-handling part of the workflow.

laboratory_instruments.question: Why is a plate reader fitted with a stacker rather than loaded by hand?

choices.A: Because the stacker improves the precision of each reading
choices.B: Because reading many plates unattended needs them fed in turn
choices.C: Because the stacker normalizes the plates against one another
choices.D: Because the reader cannot be opened once a run has started
choices.E: Because the stacker seals the plates between the readings

laboratory_instruments.explanation: The point is unattended operation: dozens of plates can be queued and read in sequence without anyone present, which is what lets a time course or a large screen run overnight. The stacker moves plates and nothing more, so it does not change the precision of a reading, normalize anything, or seal the plates.

design_and_verification_software.topic: Deciding how much to trust a generated answer
design_and_verification_software.question: You ask a language model what product your construction file yields and it returns a confident, detailed answer. What should you do with it?

choices.A: Accept it, since the file contains all the needed information
choices.B: Accept it if it agrees with what you expected the product to be
choices.C: Check it with a simulator, which computes the answer outright
choices.D: Discard it, since such tools cannot reason about sequences
choices.E: Ask again and accept the answer if the two responses agree

design_and_verification_software.explanation: This question has a determinate answer that a simulator computes from the actual sequences and the stated operations, so there is no reason to accept a prediction when you can have the result. Accepting it because it matches your expectation checks the model against the very assumption you were trying to test, and asking twice measures consistency rather than correctness.

design_and_verification_software.topic: Understanding why a full sequence cannot be inferred
design_and_verification_software.question: Why can a language model not reconstruct a plasmid's full sequence from its cloning steps and oligo table?

choices.A: Because cloning steps are always described incompletely
choices.B: Because the exact sequence depends on parts the text omits
choices.C: Because sequence prediction requires a structural model
choices.D: Because oligo tables are proprietary and withheld
choices.E: Because the model cannot perform string operations at all

design_and_verification_software.explanation: A paper names the vector and the inserts but rarely spells out every base of the backbone, every junction and every silent change, so the sequence simply is not recoverable from what is written. A simulator given the actual parent sequences and the operations can produce it exactly, which is the right tool for the job and is why construction files are written down.

design_and_verification_software.topic: Choosing between simulation and a predictive model
design_and_verification_software.question: You want to know what product a stated series of digests and ligations yields. Which tool answers that?

choices.A: A language model asked to reason through the steps
choices.B: A structure prediction tool applied to the encoded protein
choices.C: A construction file simulator applied to the parent sequences
choices.D: A BLAST search of the inserts against the parent vector
choices.E: A pathway design tool drawing on a reaction database

design_and_verification_software.explanation: This is a deterministic question about sequence manipulation, so it should be computed rather than predicted: the simulator applies each operation to the actual sequences and returns the product or an error. A language model may be right and offers no way to tell, and the other tools answer questions about homology, structure and pathways instead.

design_and_verification_software.topic: Knowing what a homology search answers
design_and_verification_software.question: What does a BLAST search tell you about a gene of interest?

choices.A: Which sequences in the databases resemble it, and how closely
choices.B: Whether the protein it encodes will fold in E. coli
choices.C: What expression level it will reach under a given promoter
choices.D: Which restriction enzymes will cut the sequence once
choices.E: What the three-dimensional structure of the product is

design_and_verification_software.explanation: A homology search reports similar sequences with alignments and scores, which is how orthologs are found for a library of natural variants and how an unknown reading frame gets a provisional annotation. It says nothing by itself about folding, expression or structure, and finding unique cut sites is an ordinary sequence search rather than a homology question.

design_and_verification_software.topic: Using homology searching to build a variant set
design_and_verification_software.question: Why search for orthologs before committing to one enzyme for a pathway?

choices.A: Because orthologs reveal the host's codon usage preferences
choices.B: Because natural variants differ in activity, stability and expression
choices.C: Because orthologs are cheaper to synthesize than the original
choices.D: Because orthologs are guaranteed to work where the original fails
choices.E: Because ortholog sequences are required for a BLAST search

design_and_verification_software.explanation: The same reaction carried out in many organisms gives you a set of sequences that already work, and they differ in exactly the properties that decide whether a pathway step performs: how fast, how stable, and how well expressed in your host. Testing several is usually cheaper than optimizing one, which is why these variant sets are built, but none of them is guaranteed.

design_and_verification_software.topic: Knowing what a sequence editor is for
design_and_verification_software.question: What role does a sequence editor play in a design workflow?

choices.A: It predicts how strongly a designed construct will express
choices.B: It simulates the thermocycling conditions of each reaction
choices.C: It holds annotated sequences and supports the editing of them
choices.D: It searches the databases for homologs of the insert
choices.E: It schedules the operations for the liquid handling robot

design_and_verification_software.explanation: The editor is where the sequences and their annotations live, and where features are inspected, sites are found and edits are made and kept track of. It is the record the rest of the tools act on, which is why the annotations being right matters so much. Prediction, homology searching and scheduling are all handled elsewhere.

design_and_verification_software.topic: Judging what a structure prediction supports
design_and_verification_software.question: A structure prediction gives a confident model of your enzyme. What does that support?

choices.A: A claim that the enzyme is active on the new substrate
choices.B: A prediction of the titer the pathway will reach
choices.C: A choice of which residues to target for mutagenesis
choices.D: A conclusion that the protein will express solubly
choices.E: A measurement of the enzyme's thermal stability

design_and_verification_software.explanation: A model is most useful for deciding where to look: which residues line the pocket, which are buried, which sit at a domain interface, all of which focus a library on positions worth varying. It does not establish activity, solubility, stability or yield, every one of which is a measurement, and treating a confident model as evidence for them is the error to avoid.

design_and_verification_software.topic: Understanding what a pathway design tool produces
design_and_verification_software.question: What does a pathway design tool drawing on a reaction database give you?

choices.A: A candidate route from an available substrate to the target
choices.B: The expression levels each enzyme in the route will need
choices.C: An assurance that the route will carry flux in the host
choices.D: The sequences of the enzymes, verified for the chosen host
choices.E: A construction file for assembling the pathway genes

design_and_verification_software.explanation: The tool searches known reactions for a chain connecting something the host already makes to the compound you want, and returns the chemistry of a candidate route. Whether that route actually carries flux, what expression each step needs, which enzyme sequences to use, and how to build it are all downstream questions, and the first of them is settled only at the bench.

design_and_verification_software.topic: Placing verification between design and the bench
design_and_verification_software.question: Where does construction file simulation sit in the design-build-test-learn cycle?

choices.A: In the test phase, as an alternative to assaying the construct
choices.B: Outside the cycle, as a purely documentary exercise
choices.C: In the learn phase, explaining why a construct behaved oddly
choices.D: After the build, confirming that the clone is correct
choices.E: Between design and build, checking the plan before execution

design_and_verification_software.explanation: Simulation is a check on the plan, so it belongs after the design is written and before any reagent is consumed, which is what makes the error it catches cheap. Confirming that the clone you actually built is correct is a separate step done by sequencing, and no simulation substitutes for assaying what the construct does.

design_and_verification_software.topic: Matching a computational tool to the question
design_and_verification_software.question: You must find a unique restriction site in a 6 kb plasmid for a planned insertion. Which tool fits?

choices.A: A language model asked to read the published map
choices.B: A homology search of the plasmid against the databases
choices.C: A structure prediction of the encoded protein product
choices.D: A pathway design tool searching a reaction database
choices.E: A sequence editor searching the sequence for cut sites

design_and_verification_software.explanation: Finding where an enzyme cuts and how many times is an exact search over a sequence you already have, which an editor does definitively and in a moment. A language model reading a map may be right without any way to confirm it, and homology, structure and pathway tools are addressed to entirely different questions.

design_and_verification_software.topic: Sorting questions a model can answer from ones it cannot
design_and_verification_software.question: You give a language model a paper describing a cellulase expressed from a T7 promoter in BL21(DE3). Which question is it most likely to answer correctly?

choices.A: What fraction of the expressed enzyme ends up in inclusion bodies
choices.B: Which inducer the construct needs, given its promoter and strain
choices.C: Which single residue change would broaden the substrate range
choices.D: How many hours of induction give the highest activity
choices.E: What turnover number the enzyme reaches on this substrate

design_and_verification_software.explanation: One of these follows from what the paper already names: the promoter and the strain between them fix the induction chemistry, and no measurement is needed to say so. The rest are predictions about how a particular protein behaves in a particular host, and each would be settled by an experiment rather than by reading. Solubility, the effect of a substitution, a time course and a kinetic constant are all quantities the text does not contain, so a confident answer about any of them is generated rather than derived. The test is not whether the question sounds technical but whether the answer is already present in what was supplied.

prototyping_versus_optimization.topic: Judging what makes a first-round result useful
prototyping_versus_optimization.question: A first circuit gives output well below target, but it tracks inducer concentration in the direction and roughly the shape predicted. How should that be read?

choices.A: As a failure, since the output misses the target by a wide margin
choices.B: As inconclusive until the output reaches the specified level
choices.C: As a reason to abandon this architecture for a different one
choices.D: As a successful prototype, since the system behaves understandably
choices.E: As evidence the assay rather than the circuit needs attention

prototyping_versus_optimization.explanation: A prototype earns its keep by being interpretable, and a circuit responding in the predicted direction with roughly the predicted shape tells you the architecture works and only the magnitude needs attention, which is what later focused edits are for. A weak but well-behaved first result is a far better starting point than a strong one you cannot account for.

prototyping_versus_optimization.question: What distinguishes optimization from prototyping in the design-build-test-learn cycle?

choices.A: Optimization starts from the current best and edits it narrowly
choices.B: Optimization uses a larger library than prototyping does
choices.C: Optimization is done in cells and prototyping in extract
choices.D: Optimization requires automation and prototyping does not
choices.E: Optimization happens before the first design is built

prototyping_versus_optimization.explanation: Prototyping builds a plausible design from scratch to see what happens, while optimization takes the construct that currently works best and makes focused changes to it, measuring each one against the last. The distinction is in where the design comes from and how far it moves, not in the format, the scale or the equipment used.

prototyping_versus_optimization.topic: Explaining why part boundaries are designed in advance
prototyping_versus_optimization.question: Why is it worth defining clean part boundaries and editable junctions in a first construct?

choices.A: Because they raise the expression level of the assembled circuit
choices.B: Because they reduce the number of transformants needed
choices.C: Because boundaries are required for the construct to be simulated
choices.D: Because later optimization means swapping parts one at a time
choices.E: Because they prevent recombination between repeated sequences

prototyping_versus_optimization.explanation: Optimization proceeds by changing one element and measuring, which is cheap if the promoter or the ribosome binding site can be exchanged on its own and expensive if the construct has to be rebuilt each time. Designing those seams in before you know which part you will want to change is what makes the later rounds fast, and it costs nothing at the first build.

prototyping_versus_optimization.topic: Knowing what each phase of the cycle contributes
prototyping_versus_optimization.question: In the design-build-test-learn cycle, what does the learn phase contribute?

choices.A: The assembled construct, ready to be assayed in the host
choices.B: The measurements of how the construct actually performed
choices.C: The specification the finished system has to satisfy
choices.D: The verification that the construct matches its design
choices.E: A revised understanding that changes the next design

prototyping_versus_optimization.explanation: Measurement is the test phase; learning is what you do with it, which is to revise your picture of the system so that the next design differs for a reason. A cycle that measures and then builds the next version without that step is iterating rather than learning, and tends to wander. The construct and its verification belong to the build.

prototyping_versus_optimization.topic: Recognizing an early design judged by the wrong standard
prototyping_versus_optimization.question: A reviewer rejects a first-round circuit because its output falls short of the production target. What is wrong with that judgment?

choices.A: Nothing, since a design that misses its target has failed
choices.B: The target cannot be assessed without fermentation data
choices.C: A first design is built to be informative, not to hit a target
choices.D: The output should be normalized before it is compared
choices.E: Production targets apply only to pathways, not to circuits

prototyping_versus_optimization.explanation: Holding a prototype to a production specification mistakes which phase the work is in. The question to ask of a first design is whether it behaves understandably and tells you what to change, and a circuit that is weak but responds as predicted is a good prototype. Normalization matters for comparing measurements but is not what makes the judgment wrong.

prototyping_versus_optimization.topic: Knowing when to move from prototyping to optimization
prototyping_versus_optimization.question: What indicates that a project should move from prototyping into optimization?

choices.A: The first construct has been sequence verified successfully
choices.B: Automation has been set up for the construction workflow
choices.C: The available library size has been fully screened through
choices.D: A design behaves predictably and the limiting step is identified
choices.E: The output has reached the production specification already

prototyping_versus_optimization.explanation: Optimization is focused editing, and it pays only once you know what to edit, which means the system behaves in a way you can anticipate and you can say which step is holding the output back. Before that, further focused edits are guesses. Reaching the specification would mean the work is finished rather than entering a new phase.

prototyping_versus_optimization.topic: Reasoning about designing for later edits
prototyping_versus_optimization.question: Why design a vector so that a promoter can be replaced without rebuilding the whole construct?

choices.A: Because promoters are the only part worth varying later
choices.B: Because the vector will otherwise recombine during growth
choices.C: Because each optimization round then costs one cloning step
choices.D: Because replacing a promoter requires unique flanking sites
choices.E: Because the construct cannot otherwise be sequence verified

prototyping_versus_optimization.explanation: The economics of optimization are set by what each iteration costs, and a construct whose promoter sits between usable unique sites can be retuned with a single digest and ligation rather than a fresh assembly. Promoters are not the only part worth varying, which is an argument for designing several such seams rather than for ignoring them.

prototyping_versus_optimization.topic: Extracting information from a design that did not work
prototyping_versus_optimization.question: A prototype produces no detectable output at all. What is the most useful next step?

choices.A: Rebuild the same design and assay it a second time
choices.B: Move directly to optimizing the strongest available promoter
choices.C: Abandon the architecture and design a different circuit
choices.D: Test the parts separately to find which step is failing
choices.E: Raise the plasmid copy number and reassay the construct

prototyping_versus_optimization.explanation: A null result does not say where the fault lies, so the informative move is to decompose it: confirm that the reporter can be seen at all, that the promoter fires, and that each part behaves as a part before asking the assembly to work. Rebuilding unchanged tests reproducibility rather than cause, and tuning or abandoning the design commits before you know what is broken.

prototyping_versus_optimization.topic: Placing cell-free work within the cycle
prototyping_versus_optimization.question: Why does cell-free expression sit naturally in the prototyping phase rather than in optimization?

choices.A: Because extracts give higher output than living cells do
choices.B: Because it tests parts quickly, without the context they will face
choices.C: Because optimization requires linkage that extracts cannot provide
choices.D: Because extracts cannot express more than one gene at a time
choices.E: Because prototypes are always built from linear DNA templates

prototyping_versus_optimization.explanation: Prototyping asks whether the parts do roughly what you think, and an extract answers that in hours from a PCR product, stripped of growth and native regulation. Optimization is about performance in the context the system will actually run in, so it has to be done there. Extracts do not outperform cells on yield and are not limited to a single gene.

prototyping_versus_optimization.topic: Reasoning about what sets the pace of the cycle
prototyping_versus_optimization.question: What most directly determines how many design-build-test-learn rounds a project can run?

choices.A: The theoretical diversity of the libraries being constructed
choices.B: The sequencing platform chosen for verifying each construct
choices.C: The number of parts in the registry available for use
choices.D: The time and cost of completing one full turn of the cycle
choices.E: The transformation efficiency of the chosen host strain

prototyping_versus_optimization.explanation: Rounds are the currency of this kind of work, and how many you get is set by how long and how much one of them takes, which is why so much effort goes into shortening the build and test steps through cloning strategy, automation and cell-free triage. Library diversity, part availability and transformation efficiency bear on individual steps rather than on the pace of the loop.

risk_groups_and_select_agents.topic: Understanding what a risk group classification means
risk_groups_and_select_agents.question: What does an organism's risk group describe?

choices.A: The hazard it presents to the individuals working with it
choices.B: The probability that it will escape the laboratory entirely
choices.C: The chemical hazard of the compounds it is engineered to make
choices.D: The monetary value of the research it is being used for
choices.E: The level of government approval its use requires in writing

risk_groups_and_select_agents.explanation: The risk groups rank organisms by the hazard they pose in a laboratory exposure, from agents unlikely to cause disease in healthy adults up through those causing severe disease with no available treatment. Containment requirements follow from the classification rather than defining it, and the chemistry of what the organism produces is assessed separately.

risk_groups_and_select_agents.question: How is the risk group of an engineered strain determined?

choices.A: By the host strain alone, since the inserts are not organisms
choices.B: By the worst of the host and whatever has been put into it
choices.C: By averaging the risk groups of the host and the inserts
choices.D: By the containment level of the laboratory it is used in
choices.E: By the risk group of the organism the insert came from

risk_groups_and_select_agents.explanation: Taking a harmless host and giving it a virulence determinant produces something more hazardous than the host was, so the classification has to account for both the chassis and its cargo and settles on the more serious of them. Neither the host alone nor the donor alone decides it, and the laboratory's containment is what the classification obliges rather than what sets it.

risk_groups_and_select_agents.question: A non-pathogenic E. coli is engineered to make a flammable hydrocarbon using genes from soil bacteria. What is its risk group?

choices.A: RG2, because the product presents a hazard to workers
choices.B: A select agent, because fuels have potential for misuse
choices.C: RG1, because no biological hazard has been added
choices.D: RG3, because flammable products require stronger containment
choices.E: It cannot be classified until the product is characterized

risk_groups_and_select_agents.explanation: The host is harmless and the donors are non-pathogenic, so nothing has been added that makes the organism more dangerous to the people handling it. The flammability of the product is a real hazard and is managed as a chemical one, with the appropriate storage and fire precautions, but it does not move the strain's biological classification.

risk_groups_and_select_agents.topic: Reasoning about a virulence determinant in a safe host
risk_groups_and_select_agents.question: A routine cloning strain is engineered to display a functional adhesin that lets it attach to and invade human epithelial cells. How should it be classified?

choices.A: RG1, since the parent cloning strain is itself harmless
choices.B: RG3, since the donor organism causes serious disease
choices.C: A select agent, because an invasion gene has been moved
choices.D: RG2, since the added function raises what an exposure could do
choices.E: Unclassifiable, since adhesins act only on cultured cell lines

risk_groups_and_select_agents.explanation: The chassis was innocuous and now carries a function that lets it enter human cells, which changes what an accidental exposure could lead to and so lifts the classification above the host's own. It does not simply inherit the donor's classification, since one determinant is not the whole pathogen, and nothing in the description raises the deliberate-misuse concern that defines a select agent.

risk_groups_and_select_agents.question: What distinguishes a select agent from an organism that is merely high risk group?

choices.A: Its requirement for a biosafety cabinet during handling
choices.B: Its resistance to the antibiotics used in the laboratory
choices.C: Its potential for deliberate misuse against people or crops
choices.D: Its ability to survive outside the laboratory environment
choices.E: Its classification by the institution rather than by statute

risk_groups_and_select_agents.explanation: Risk group speaks to accidental harm to a worker, while the select agent lists exist because an agent could be used deliberately to cause mass harm, which brings registration, inventory control and personnel vetting with it. Containment equipment, drug resistance and environmental persistence may accompany such agents without being what puts them on the list.

risk_groups_and_select_agents.topic: Classifying an agent by its misuse potential
risk_groups_and_select_agents.question: A plant pathogen capable of destroying a staple cereal crop is on a federal list requiring registration, inventory control and personnel vetting. What does that status reflect?

choices.A: That it is classified in the highest risk group available
choices.B: That no treatment exists for the disease it causes
choices.C: That it is assessed as a target for deliberate misuse
choices.D: That it requires the strictest containment to handle safely
choices.E: That it cannot be transferred between institutions at all

risk_groups_and_select_agents.explanation: Registration, inventory control and vetting of the people with access are the controls attached to agents judged capable of being used deliberately to cause mass harm, to people, livestock or crops. That is a different question from how dangerous the organism is to the person handling it, which is what risk group and containment level describe, and an agent can be hazardous in a laboratory without appearing on such a list.

risk_groups_and_select_agents.topic: Distinguishing risk group from biosafety level
risk_groups_and_select_agents.question: How do risk group and biosafety level differ?

choices.A: Risk group ranks the agent; biosafety level describes the practices
choices.B: They are the same scale under two different names
choices.C: Risk group applies to bacteria and biosafety level to viruses
choices.D: Risk group is assigned locally and biosafety level nationally
choices.E: Risk group covers accidents and biosafety level covers misuse

risk_groups_and_select_agents.explanation: One classifies the agent and the other prescribes how work with it is conducted: the facility, the equipment and the procedures. They usually correspond, but not always, because the containment required also depends on what is being done, so a procedure generating aerosols with a lower risk group agent may be carried out at a higher containment level.

risk_groups_and_select_agents.topic: Reasoning about a deliberately weakened host
risk_groups_and_select_agents.question: Why are laboratory E. coli strains such as the common cloning hosts treated as low risk?

choices.A: Because they cannot take up foreign DNA from the environment
choices.B: Because they carry mutations leaving them poorly able to colonize
choices.C: Because they are killed by the antibiotics used in the medium
choices.D: Because they grow only at temperatures below body temperature
choices.E: Because they lack the ability to replicate plasmids efficiently

risk_groups_and_select_agents.explanation: Decades of laboratory passage and deliberate modification have left these strains dependent on rich medium and poor at colonizing a human gut, which is a large part of why routine cloning is low risk work. They take up DNA readily, which is the point of them, replicate plasmids well, and grow perfectly happily at body temperature.

risk_groups_and_select_agents.question: At what point should an engineered strain's risk classification be settled?

choices.A: After the first results indicate whether it is hazardous
choices.B: Before the work begins, as part of the approval for it
choices.C: At publication, when the construct is described in full
choices.D: Whenever an exposure incident occurs in the laboratory
choices.E: Only if the strain is to be transferred to another laboratory

risk_groups_and_select_agents.explanation: The classification determines where the work may be done, what equipment is required and what training the people need, all of which have to be in place before anyone handles the organism. Deciding afterward means the work has already been done at whatever containment happened to be convenient, and an incident is the worst possible moment to discover the answer.

risk_groups_and_select_agents.topic: Recognizing when a modification changes the classification
risk_groups_and_select_agents.question: Which modification to an RG1 host would most clearly require reassessment of its classification?

choices.A: Codon optimizing an existing gene for better expression
choices.B: Replacing the plasmid origin with a higher copy number one
choices.C: Adding a gene conferring resistance to a clinical antibiotic
choices.D: Adding a fluorescent protein for tracking the strain
choices.E: Adding a terminator downstream of the reporter gene

risk_groups_and_select_agents.explanation: Resistance to a drug used to treat human infection changes what an exposure would mean and how an infection could be managed, which is a change in hazard rather than in performance. Codon changes, copy number, reporters and terminators all alter how the construct behaves without altering what harm the organism could do to a person.

controls_and_oversight.question: A rule requires two people to sign the inventory before a regulated strain leaves the freezer. What kind of control is that?
