choices.A: An engineering control, since the freezer restricts access
choices.B: Personal protective equipment for the people handling it
choices.C: An administrative control, being a procedure governing the work
choices.D: A biological containment measure applied to the strain
choices.E: A procedural control carried out during the experiment

controls_and_oversight.explanation: Administrative controls are the policies that govern who may do what and under what conditions, and a required countersignature is exactly that: it constrains the work rather than containing the hazard. A lock on the freezer would be an engineering control addressing the same concern, and the distinction matters because the two fail in different ways.

controls_and_oversight.topic: Classifying the screening of synthesis orders
controls_and_oversight.question: A synthesis company checks incoming orders against sequences of concern. What kind of control is that?

choices.A: An engineering control, since it is performed by software
choices.B: An administrative control, being a policy applied to the work
choices.C: Personal protective equipment for the people synthesizing
choices.D: A procedural control applied after the synthesis is complete
choices.E: A biological containment measure built into the product

controls_and_oversight.explanation: Screening is a policy that governs what work is accepted, applied before anything is made, which puts it with training and standard procedures among the administrative controls. That it is implemented in software does not make it an engineering control, since engineering controls are physical features of the workplace such as cabinets and ventilation.

controls_and_oversight.question: Which pair are both engineering controls?

choices.A: A biosafety cabinet and a kill switch in the organism
choices.B: A respirator and a standard operating procedure
choices.C: Required training and an autoclave cycle for waste
choices.D: A laboratory coat and a signed use authorization
choices.E: Gloves and a sequence screening policy for orders

controls_and_oversight.explanation: Engineering controls are features built into the equipment or the organism so that safety does not rely on someone remembering: a cabinet that contains aerosols, interlocks, directional airflow, and biological containment such as a kill switch or an auxotrophy. Respirators, coats and gloves protect the individual wearing them, and training, procedures and screening are administrative.

controls_and_oversight.topic: Reasoning about why control types are ranked
controls_and_oversight.question: Why is an engineering control generally preferred to personal protective equipment for the same hazard?

choices.A: It costs less to install than the equipment costs to supply
choices.B: It protects without depending on correct use each time
choices.C: It is required by regulation where equipment is optional
choices.D: It removes the need for any administrative controls
choices.E: It protects the individual rather than the whole laboratory

controls_and_oversight.explanation: Protective equipment works only when it is worn, worn properly and changed when it should be, which puts a human decision between the hazard and the person every single time. A cabinet or an interlock contains the hazard whether or not anyone is paying attention, which is why the hierarchy puts it higher, and it protects everyone in the room rather than one wearer.

controls_and_oversight.topic: Knowing what a biological use authorization covers
controls_and_oversight.question: What is a biological use authorization?

choices.A: A certificate that the laboratory's cabinet has been serviced
choices.B: Institutional approval to perform specified work with an agent
choices.C: A permit issued by a national agency for each experiment
choices.D: A record of training completed by every laboratory member
choices.E: A license required to purchase a regulated organism

controls_and_oversight.explanation: It is the institution's written approval of a described piece of work, covering the agents, the procedures, the containment and the people, and it has to be in place before the work begins. Equipment certification and training records support the application rather than constituting it, and it is an institutional authorization rather than a per-experiment national permit.

controls_and_oversight.topic: Knowing who reviews work of this kind
controls_and_oversight.question: Who reviews a proposal to work with recombinant organisms at a university?

choices.A: The journal's editors at the point of publication
choices.B: The funding agency's program officers, during review
choices.C: An institutional biosafety committee established for the purpose
choices.D: The laboratory's own members, by internal agreement
choices.E: The national regulator, which reviews each proposal directly

controls_and_oversight.explanation: Review sits with a standing institutional committee that includes biosafety expertise and members from outside the research group, and it is that body which authorizes the work and sets conditions on it. Funders and journals assess merit and reporting rather than containment, and national frameworks generally operate through such local committees instead of reviewing every project centrally.

controls_and_oversight.topic: Distinguishing a procedural step from a policy
controls_and_oversight.question: Autoclaving waste is often called a procedural control rather than an administrative one. What is the distinction?

choices.A: It is performed by equipment rather than by a person
choices.B: It applies to waste rather than to the live organism
choices.C: It is a step within the work, not a policy governing it
choices.D: It is optional, whereas administrative controls are required
choices.E: It is verified by indicators, whereas policies are not

controls_and_oversight.explanation: Administrative controls decide what work may be done, by whom, and under what conditions, while a procedural control is an operation inside that work, carried out at the bench each time. The requirement that waste be autoclaved is itself administrative; the autoclaving is the procedure that satisfies it, which is why the two are easy to run together.

controls_and_oversight.topic: Choosing controls for a specific hazard
controls_and_oversight.question: A procedure on an RG2 organism generates aerosols. Which combination addresses that?

choices.A: Gloves and a laboratory coat, changed between procedures
choices.B: Training in the procedure, plus autoclaving of the waste
choices.C: A cabinet containing the aerosol, with procedure and training
choices.D: A kill switch engineered into the organism being handled
choices.E: A signed use authorization naming the procedure performed

controls_and_oversight.explanation: The hazard is airborne, so the first line is a physical barrier that captures the aerosol at source, supported by a written procedure for working in it and training in that procedure. Gloves and a coat do not protect against inhalation, waste handling addresses a different route, a kill switch addresses release rather than exposure, and an authorization permits the work without containing anything.

controls_and_oversight.topic: Reasoning about dependence on human compliance
controls_and_oversight.question: Which control continues to protect if the person performing the work forgets a step?

choices.A: A standard operating procedure describing the correct steps
choices.B: Required annual training in handling the organism
choices.C: A record kept of each procedure as it is performed
choices.D: A policy requiring waste to be autoclaved before disposal
choices.E: A cabinet whose airflow contains material regardless

controls_and_oversight.explanation: This is the reason the hierarchy exists. Procedures, training, policies and records all work through someone doing the right thing, and they fail together the moment attention lapses. Directional airflow in a cabinet keeps containing material whether or not anyone is thinking about it, which is what makes an engineering control the more robust answer to the same hazard.

controls_and_oversight.topic: Connecting order screening to misuse concerns
controls_and_oversight.question: Why do synthesis providers screen orders rather than relying on the purchaser's institution?

choices.A: Because institutions lack the sequence databases required
choices.B: Because screening is cheaper to perform at the provider
choices.C: Because institutional committees review only published work
choices.D: Because synthesis is the point where a sequence becomes material
choices.E: Because purchasers are not obliged to disclose their intent

controls_and_oversight.explanation: A hazardous sequence is only information until someone makes DNA out of it, so the synthesis step is the natural chokepoint at which a control can act, and it catches orders that never pass any institutional review. That is a reason of position rather than of capability, and the control works alongside institutional oversight rather than in place of it.

release_dual_use_and_perception.question: An assessment must address whether an engineered strain could persist outside the laboratory. What evidence speaks to that?

choices.A: Its growth rate in rich medium at thirty-seven degrees
choices.B: The copy number of the plasmid it carries in culture
choices.C: The brightness of its reporter when the inducer is present
choices.D: Survival in environmental samples at ambient temperature
choices.E: Its transformation efficiency when made chemically competent

release_dual_use_and_perception.explanation: Persistence is a question about the conditions the organism would actually meet, so the informative experiment puts it into those conditions: soil or water from the site, at ambient temperature, with the nutrients available there, followed over time. Laboratory growth in rich medium at body temperature is the measurement that tells you least about this, since it is the condition the strain was domesticated for.

release_dual_use_and_perception.topic: Understanding why gene exchange is assessed
release_dual_use_and_perception.question: Why does an assessment ask whether a released organism could exchange genes with native species?

choices.A: Because transfer would dilute the construct and reduce performance
choices.B: Because native species cannot take up plasmid DNA at all
choices.C: Because recipients would become classifiable as select agents
choices.D: Because transfer would prevent the organism from being recovered
choices.E: Because an introduced gene could persist even if the host does not

release_dual_use_and_perception.explanation: The engineered strain may well die out, but a resistance marker or a metabolic function it carried can move into organisms that are already established and stay in the environment indefinitely. That makes the consequence outlast the organism, which is why transfer is assessed separately from survival, and it is part of why markers are chosen carefully for anything intended to leave containment.

release_dual_use_and_perception.question: Which approach is a biological containment measure for an organism intended to leave the laboratory?

choices.A: Autoclaving the culture before it is taken to the field
choices.B: Requiring the operators to wear gloves while sampling
choices.C: Making the strain dependent on a compound not found in nature
choices.D: Obtaining an institutional authorization for the field work
choices.E: Keeping the organism in a sealed cartridge during sampling

release_dual_use_and_perception.explanation: Engineering a dependence on a synthetic nutrient, or a kill switch that fires outside defined conditions, builds the limit into the organism so that escape does not become establishment. A sealed cartridge is a genuine physical containment that may well be the right answer for a field device, but it is engineering rather than biological containment, and authorizations and gloves address other things entirely.

release_dual_use_and_perception.topic: Defining dual use research of concern
release_dual_use_and_perception.question: What makes a piece of research dual use?

choices.A: It is funded by both civilian and military sources
choices.B: Its results are published in two different fields at once
choices.C: Its findings could enable harm as readily as benefit
choices.D: It uses organisms classified in two different risk groups
choices.E: It can be performed in either academic or industrial settings

release_dual_use_and_perception.explanation: The concern is about the knowledge rather than the funding or the venue: work done for an entirely legitimate reason may also tell someone how to make a pathogen more transmissible, more virulent, or harder to treat. That is why the question is asked of the findings and their publication rather than of the investigator's motives, and why it arises in ordinary laboratories.

release_dual_use_and_perception.topic: Understanding what makes a gene drive different
release_dual_use_and_perception.question: What distinguishes a gene drive from an ordinary engineered trait in a wild population?

choices.A: It spreads through the population faster than inheritance allows
choices.B: It persists only as long as the released individuals survive
choices.C: It can be reversed by ceasing to release the organism
choices.D: It acts on somatic cells rather than on the germ line
choices.E: It requires continuous release to maintain its frequency

release_dual_use_and_perception.explanation: A drive biases its own inheritance, so it can increase in frequency even when it carries a fitness cost and spread from a small release through a whole interbreeding population. That is precisely what makes it powerful against a disease vector and what makes it hard to recall, since stopping releases does not stop the spread the way it would for an ordinary trait.

release_dual_use_and_perception.topic: Reasoning about public perception of risk
release_dual_use_and_perception.question: Public concern about an engineered organism is far greater than the assessed risk. How should that be handled?

choices.A: As irrelevant, since the assessment is the technical answer
choices.B: As evidence the assessment has underestimated the hazard
choices.C: As a real constraint to be engaged, distinct from the hazard
choices.D: As a problem solved by withholding details of the work
choices.E: As grounds to proceed only once concern has subsided

release_dual_use_and_perception.explanation: Perception and assessed hazard are different quantities and both are real: the assessment tells you what the organism can do, and public acceptance determines whether the work can proceed at all and on what terms. Treating concern as ignorance to be overridden, or as a hazard signal in itself, both misread it, and withholding information reliably makes it worse.

release_dual_use_and_perception.topic: Distinguishing a contained field use from a release
release_dual_use_and_perception.question: A whole-cell biosensor is used on samples brought to a sealed cartridge and autoclaved afterward. How does that change the assessment?

choices.A: It does not, since the organism has left the laboratory
choices.B: It becomes a question of containment in the field, not of release
choices.C: It removes the need for any institutional authorization
choices.D: It makes the organism's survival in the environment irrelevant
choices.E: It converts the work into dual use research of concern

release_dual_use_and_perception.explanation: Taking the sample to a contained organism is a different proposition from putting the organism into the environment, and the questions become whether the containment holds in field conditions and whether the waste is reliably inactivated. Survival outside is not irrelevant, since it is what a containment failure would mean, and authorization is still required.

release_dual_use_and_perception.topic: Reasoning about marker choice for release
release_dual_use_and_perception.question: Why would an antibiotic resistance marker be avoided in an organism intended for environmental use?

choices.A: Because resistance genes are unstable outside the laboratory
choices.B: Because the antibiotic cannot be supplied in the field
choices.C: Because the marker could transfer and persist in the environment
choices.D: Because resistance markers raise the strain's risk group
choices.E: Because markers interfere with the sensing function itself

release_dual_use_and_perception.explanation: A resistance gene is the clearest case of something whose consequences outlive the organism carrying it, since it can move into resident bacteria and remain in a setting where that resistance matters clinically. Selection in the field is a practical problem too, which is why auxotrophic or synthetic-dependency markers are preferred, but the transfer concern is the governing one.

release_dual_use_and_perception.topic: Reasoning about whether a release can be undone
release_dual_use_and_perception.question: Why is reversibility a central question for a deliberate release?

choices.A: Because regulators require a disposal plan for all materials
choices.B: Because an established population cannot simply be recalled
choices.C: Because irreversible releases are prohibited under all frameworks
choices.D: Because reversibility determines the organism's risk group
choices.E: Because an unrecoverable organism cannot be studied further

release_dual_use_and_perception.explanation: Once an organism establishes and reproduces in the environment there is often no way to withdraw it, so the decision cannot be revisited in the light of what is learned afterward, which is the opposite of how laboratory work proceeds. That asymmetry is why the assessment is made so carefully beforehand and why built-in limits on persistence carry so much weight.

release_dual_use_and_perception.topic: Reasoning about publishing dual use findings
release_dual_use_and_perception.question: A result would help defend against a pathogen and also show how to make it more transmissible. What does the dual use framework ask?

choices.A: That the work be classified and withheld from publication entirely
choices.B: That the benefit and the misuse potential be weighed before publishing
choices.C: That the work be abandoned, since the risk cannot be eliminated
choices.D: That publication proceed, since open science resolves such tensions
choices.E: That the decision be left to the journal's editors alone

release_dual_use_and_perception.explanation: The framework asks for deliberate consideration rather than a fixed answer: what the result enables for defense, what it enables for harm, who already has it, and whether some of it can be communicated differently. Automatic publication and automatic suppression both skip that judgment, and the decision involves the investigators, the institution and the funder as well as the journal.

release_dual_use_and_perception.topic: Telling the concern that gates a release from product concerns
release_dual_use_and_perception.question: An engineered strain is proposed for treating mine tailings in open settling ponds. Which question must be answered before the deployment can be approved?

choices.A: Whether it degrades the contaminant faster than the current treatment
choices.B: Whether the operators can be trained to dose the ponds correctly
choices.C: Whether the treatment costs less per ton than the current process
choices.D: Whether the strain establishes in the ponds and spreads beyond them
choices.E: Whether the process can be protected as a trade secret

release_dual_use_and_perception.explanation: Four of these decide whether the process is worth adopting and one decides whether it is permitted at all. Open ponds put live cells in contact with groundwater and wildlife, so approval turns on whether the strain persists, multiplies and moves beyond the site. Rate, cost, training and commercial protection are all real questions that a deployment clearing every biosafety requirement would still have to answer, which is what makes them the wrong category here rather than merely less important.

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.topic: Writing a reverse complement in the correct orientation
sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.question: What is the reverse complement of 5'-GGACTT-3'?

choices.A: 5'-AAGTCC-3'
choices.B: 5'-CCTGAA-3'
choices.C: 3'-GGACTT-5'
choices.D: 5'-TTCAGG-3'
choices.E: 5'-GGACTT-3'

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.explanation: Complement each base and then reverse the order, or equivalently read the complement from the other end, and write the result conventionally with the 5' end on the left. Taking the complement without reversing gives CCTGAA, reversing without complementing gives TTCAGG, and simply relabeling the ends leaves the original sequence described from the other direction rather than its partner strand.

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.topic: Understanding which part of an oligo anneals
sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.question: In a PCR oligo carrying a 5' tail, which part determines where it binds the template?

choices.A: The 3' region, which matches the template sequence
choices.B: The 5' tail, which is read first by the polymerase
choices.C: The whole oligo, since all of it must match to anneal
choices.D: The middle, where any degenerate bases are placed
choices.E: Whichever region has the higher melting temperature

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.explanation: The 3' end is where extension begins and it is the region matched to the template, so that is what sets the priming site. The 5' tail carries whatever you are adding, such as a restriction site or degenerate bases, and need not match anything, which is exactly why it is possible to add sequence that was not in the template at all.

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.topic: Reading the case convention in a construction file
sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.question: In these construction files, what does a lowercase run inside an oligo sequence indicate?

choices.A: Sequence added by the oligo rather than copied from the template
choices.B: Sequence that is degenerate at one or more positions
choices.C: Sequence that will be removed during the restriction digest
choices.D: Sequence that anneals to the template during the reaction
choices.E: Sequence that encodes the protein's active site residues

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.explanation: The case is a reading aid marking which bases the oligo contributes and which ones correspond to the template, which makes it easy to see at a glance where a site or a tag is being introduced. Whether that added sequence survives the digest depends on where it sits relative to the recognition site, and degenerate positions are marked by their own letters.

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.topic: Explaining the short flank outside a restriction site
sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.question: Why does an oligo carry a few extra bases 5' of the restriction site in its tail?

choices.A: To raise the melting temperature of the whole oligo
choices.B: Because enzymes cut poorly at the very end of a fragment
choices.C: To keep the product in frame with the downstream gene
choices.D: To provide a second site in case the first fails to cut
choices.E: To mark where the degenerate region begins in the design

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.explanation: Most restriction enzymes need some duplex on both sides of their recognition sequence to bind and cut efficiently, so a site sitting flush with the end of a PCR product is cut badly or not at all. A short flank solves that, and it is discarded along with the end of the fragment when the digest runs, which is why nothing functional should be placed there.

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.topic: Reading a construction file as named operations
sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.question: A construction file lists PCR, Digest, Digest, Ligate and Transform, each with a named product. What do the names accomplish?

choices.A: They record which enzyme was used at each separate step
choices.B: They let each operation refer to the output of an earlier one
choices.C: They indicate the order in which the steps must be performed
choices.D: They identify which products must be sequence verified
choices.E: They specify the volume of each reaction to be set up

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.explanation: Naming the product of each step turns the file into a graph rather than a list: a digest takes the PCR's product by name, the ligation takes both digests' products, and the whole thing can be simulated because every input is defined. Order is implied by those dependencies rather than by the sequence of lines, and enzymes and volumes are recorded in the step's own parameters.

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.topic: Finding a restriction site within an oligo
sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.question: An oligo reads CAGTTgaattcGGTNDWCCAatgaccgcattgcg. Which run is the EcoRI site?

choices.A: CAGTT, the five bases at the 5' end of the oligo
choices.B: gaattc, the lowercase run following the short flank
choices.C: GGTNDWCCA, the run containing the degenerate bases
choices.D: atgaccgcattgcg, the region matching the template
choices.E: TNDW, the degenerate positions taken by themselves

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.explanation: EcoRI recognizes GAATTC, which appears here as the lowercase run just inside the short flank, placing it where the enzyme can cut with a few bases on either side. The leading CAGTT is that flank, the degenerate stretch is the library region, and the lowercase-to-uppercase transition near the end marks where the oligo begins matching the template.

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.question: In the stretch GGTNDWCCA, which expression gives the number of distinct sequences it represents?

choices.A: 4 x 3 x 2, for the N, D and W positions
choices.B: 4 + 3 + 2, summing the options at those positions
choices.C: 9^3, the length raised to the number of codes
choices.D: 3^9, three options at each of nine positions
choices.E: 4 x 3 x 2 x 9, including the fixed bases as well

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.explanation: Only three positions vary, with N standing for four bases, D for three and W for two, so the diversity is their product and the fixed bases contribute a factor of one each. Adding gives the number of choices rather than combinations, including the fixed positions multiplies by nine for no reason, and the two exponential forms invert bases and positions.

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.topic: Reasoning about how a reverse oligo is written
sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.question: A reverse oligo is listed as CCATAgaattcTTATATTGACAGCGCACAGAG. How does its 3' region relate to the published top strand?

choices.A: It matches the top strand exactly over that region
choices.B: It is the reverse complement of the top strand there
choices.C: It is the complement of the top strand without reversal
choices.D: It matches the top strand read in the 3' to 5' direction
choices.E: It is unrelated, since reverse oligos carry only tails

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.explanation: A reverse oligo primes on the top strand and extends back along it, so the sequence written in the file, read conventionally 5' to 3', is the reverse complement of the top strand across its annealing region. Expecting it to match the top strand is the usual confusion, and it is why a reverse oligo looks unfamiliar when compared directly against the published sequence.

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.question: A PCR product carries a flank, then a BamHI site, then a degenerate region, then template-matching sequence. After digestion with BamHI, what remains in the insert?

choices.A: The flank and the site, with the degenerate region removed
choices.B: Only the template-matching region, with the tail removed
choices.C: The degenerate region and the sequence inward of it
choices.D: The whole product, since digestion removes nothing
choices.E: The flank only, released as a short separate fragment

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.explanation: The enzyme cuts within its recognition sequence, so everything outside the site, meaning the short flank, is released as a tiny fragment and discarded, while everything inward of the cut stays with the insert. That is why the degenerate region must sit between the site and the annealing region: placed outside the site, it would leave with the flank and the library would be lost.

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.topic: Explaining the purpose of writing the construction down
sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.question: Why record a cloning plan as a construction file rather than as prose in a notebook?

choices.A: Because prose descriptions cannot record oligo sequences
choices.B: Because it can be simulated and executed exactly as written
choices.C: Because journals require this format for published methods
choices.D: Because it removes the need to sequence verify the product
choices.E: Because it guarantees the resulting construct will function

sequence_and_construction_file_fundament.explanation: A file with explicit operations, named products and the actual sequences is something a program can apply, which both predicts the product and catches a plan that does not do what its author thought. It is also unambiguous for whoever repeats it. Prose can contain the same sequences while leaving the operations open to interpretation, and no plan removes the need to verify the clone.

matching_method_to_scale.topic: Choosing a workflow for a few variants
matching_method_to_scale.question: You have eight defined promoter variants to characterize individually. What fits?

choices.A: Build each, pick a colony of each, and assay them in tubes
choices.B: Build a pooled library and sort the brightest by cytometry
choices.C: Array a picked library into plates with a colony picker
choices.D: Run a selection on a resistance marker and sequence survivors
choices.E: Barcode each variant and count transcripts by sequencing

matching_method_to_scale.explanation: Eight is a number you can simply handle: build each on purpose, grow it, measure it, and keep it as a named strain. Everything heavier exists to cope with numbers you cannot handle individually, and applying a pooled method here means doing extra work to recover identities you already had.

matching_method_to_scale.topic: Choosing a workflow at the thousand scale
matching_method_to_scale.question: You need a per-variant value for roughly three thousand clones. What fits?

choices.A: Picking and assaying each clone by hand in tubes
choices.B: A pooled growth selection, sequencing the survivors
choices.C: A colony picker arraying into plates, read on a plate reader
choices.D: Scraping the library and sorting the brightest fraction
choices.E: Cycle sequencing each clone to infer its activity

matching_method_to_scale.explanation: Three thousand is beyond what anyone wants to pipette by hand and well within what a picker and a few dozen plates handle, which is exactly the regime laboratory automation was built for. The pooled approaches would discard the per-variant values that were asked for, and sequencing reports identity rather than activity.

matching_method_to_scale.topic: Choosing a workflow when many winners are wanted
matching_method_to_scale.question: From a library of about a million you want the best several hundred variants, not just the single best. What fits?

choices.A: Array the whole library into plates and rank every clone
choices.B: Pick several hundred colonies at random and rank those
choices.C: Run a growth selection and keep every surviving colony
choices.D: Sort the top fraction and sequence the sorted pool as a whole
choices.E: Inspect the plate by eye and pick the several hundred brightest

matching_method_to_scale.explanation: Wanting many winners rather than one changes what the readout must do: sorting the top fraction and sequencing it as a pool reports which variants are enriched among the best performers, which is a set rather than a champion. Arraying a million clones is out of reach, random picks sample a fraction of a percent, and a survival selection returns everything above a threshold without ranking it.

matching_method_to_scale.topic: Recognizing a method heavier than the question requires
matching_method_to_scale.question: You need expression values for twelve named constructs. Why not barcode them and count transcripts by sequencing?

choices.A: Because barcodes cannot be designed for only twelve members
choices.B: Because twelve constructs cannot be pooled in one culture
choices.C: Because the method costs far more effort than reading twelve wells
choices.D: Because sequencing cannot resolve twelve barcodes reliably
choices.E: Because transcript counts do not report expression level

matching_method_to_scale.explanation: The pooled readout is a solution to not being able to measure members separately, and with twelve you can, in a single plate, for a fraction of the effort and cost. Choosing the heavier method is as much a mismatch as choosing one that cannot reach the scale, which is the symmetry worth noticing. Each of the technical objections offered is false.

matching_method_to_scale.topic: Reasoning about enrichment before individual handling
matching_method_to_scale.question: Why does a sort precede plating and rescreening rather than replacing it?

choices.A: Because sorting enriches a population without identifying clones
choices.B: Because a sorter cannot distinguish bright cells reliably
choices.C: Because sorted cells must be regrown before they can be read
choices.D: Because the sorter's gates must be calibrated on pure clones
choices.E: Because rescreening confirms the sorter's calibration was correct

matching_method_to_scale.explanation: A sort hands back an enriched population, not a list of winners, so you still have to isolate individuals from it and measure them to find the best one and to keep it as a strain. The two steps do different jobs: the sort makes the number tractable and the rescreen turns the population into identified clones with values attached.

matching_method_to_scale.topic: Connecting scale to the screen or selection decision
matching_method_to_scale.question: Which pairing of library size and approach is appropriate?

choices.A: Ten thousand members assayed individually in separate tubes
choices.B: Ten to the twelfth handled by arraying into microtiter plates
choices.C: Five hundred members handled by a pooled growth selection
choices.D: Ten to the ninth members handled by a pooled selection
choices.E: A million members assayed individually by hand over weeks

matching_method_to_scale.explanation: A library in the billions can only be handled as a population, which is what a selection does, so that pairing is the one that matches. Arraying cannot approach that scale, individual assays cannot reach ten thousand by hand or a million at all, and a pooled selection on five hundred members is heavier than the problem when a plate of picks would answer it.

matching_method_to_scale.topic: Reconciling the design with what can be screened
matching_method_to_scale.question: Your design has a diversity of twenty thousand and your screen reaches two thousand clones. What is the better response?

choices.A: Screen two thousand and report the best as the optimum
choices.B: Sequence the two thousand to infer the untested members
choices.C: Collect 4.6 times the diversity in transformants and rescreen
choices.D: Assume random sampling makes the two thousand representative
choices.E: Narrow the degenerate code so the design fits the screen

matching_method_to_scale.explanation: Only a tenth of the design can be looked at, so the honest options are to shrink the design until the screen covers it, using a weight matrix or fewer degenerate positions, or to switch to a selection that handles the whole population. Collecting more transformants fixes coverage of the library in the freezer rather than of the assay, and a sampled maximum is not the true one.

matching_method_to_scale.topic: Identifying which step limits an experiment
matching_method_to_scale.question: A library of fifty thousand is built, fully covered in transformants, and assayed clone by clone at five hundred clones per week. What limits the experiment?

choices.A: The transformation, which bounds the variants in hand
choices.B: The sequencing depth needed to confirm the library
choices.C: The construction, which must be repeated for each variant
choices.D: The coverage, which is insufficient at this diversity
choices.E: The assay throughput, which would take two years to finish

matching_method_to_scale.explanation: Coverage is stated to be adequate and the library exists, so the library is not the problem; fifty thousand clones at five hundred a week is about two years, which is the constraint that actually bites. Recognizing which step is binding is what tells you whether to change the design, the assay or the approach, and here it points at replacing the clone-by-clone assay.

matching_method_to_scale.topic: Choosing a pooled method that still returns per-variant values
matching_method_to_scale.question: You need a value for each of fifty thousand promoter variants, which is too many to array. What approach returns per-variant values?

choices.A: A growth selection, reporting which variants survived the drug
choices.B: A sort, keeping the brightest fraction for further work
choices.C: Barcoded transcript counting, normalized against input DNA
choices.D: Cycle sequencing of a few hundred picked colonies
choices.E: A plate reader measurement of the pooled culture

matching_method_to_scale.explanation: A pooled measurement that counts a tag per variant gives a number for every member rather than a surviving subset, which is what distinguishes it from a selection or a sort. Dividing message counts by the barcode's share of the input DNA turns those counts into expression levels. Picking a few hundred samples under one percent of the library, and a bulk reading returns one number for everything.

matching_method_to_scale.topic: Placing the scale decision in the workflow
matching_method_to_scale.question: At what point is the scale of the workflow decided, and by what?

choices.A: After transformation, by how many colonies were recovered
choices.B: After sequencing, by how well the library was represented
choices.C: After the first assays, by how variable the results proved
choices.D: At the readout stage, by which instrument is available
choices.E: At the design stage, by the diversity and the values required

matching_method_to_scale.explanation: Two things settle it and both are known before any DNA is made: how many members the design has, and whether you need a value for each one or only the best few. Those decide whether the work is a handful of tubes, an arrayed screen, a pooled counting experiment or a selection, and deciding afterward risks building a library you have no way to interrogate.
